title: I Tried 'Tailscale,' the Self-Hosted VPN Service That Makes It Look Like You're Always Home
description: Tailscale is a free app that's well worth setting up on phones and computers.
fullText:
Tailscale wasn't on my radar until a friend recently raved about its capabilities to me. Looking around the web, it seems the software has attracted a loyal following; perhaps part of the reason I hadn't come across it before is that it's not all that easy to understand what it does. Tailscale is technically a VPN (Virtual Private Network), but not in the way the term is typically used. Whereas something like NordVPN or ExpressVPN connects you to someone else's network to access the wider web, Tailscale does the opposite, and connects you to your own network from outside.

"Remote access technology" has been around for years, of course, but it often involves a lot of detailed and technical setup steps—you want to be able to access your home network remotely without letting anyone else in, and that usually means some complicated configuration involving router settings and several third-party apps.

There's none of that with Tailscale, and when you actually install the software, you quickly start to see what all the fuss is about. You can be sitting in a coffee shop or hotel room and have virtually the same access to your home network as you would if you were actually in your living room, which has all kinds of benefits, from file sharing to managing your smart home devices.

The obvious use case is remote access to a computer you have at home, without the layers of complexity or using another company's servers. Tailscale also makes it easier to access media servers you've set up with apps like Plex or Jellyfin, and smart home setups running through Home Assistant or another dashboard.

Everything is built on the open-source WireGuard VPN protocol, which creates private and encrypted links to all of the devices you want to connect to your network—your "tailnet." To add a new device, just install Tailscale on it, whether it's your phone on a 5G connection or a desktop computer set up at the office. Tailscale is free for personal use, which covers up to six individual users and an unlimited number of personal devices, though there are some limits: 50 tagged resources (always-on devices that need multi-user access, like a NAS box), and three Access Control List or ACL groups (for setting access permissions per user). Paid plans start at $8 per month.

The ease of setup is one of the main appeals of Tailscale, and it couldn't be much more straightforward. Download the relevant app on whatever device you want to start with, create an account (you can sign in using a Google, Microsoft, GitHub, or Apple account), and you're up and running. I had a Windows PC, a MacBook, an Android phone, and an iPhone connected to my tailnet in a matter of minutes, with just a few taps and clicks required. There's also a web portal you can access to see all of the devices you've connected and what they're up to.

One improvement I noticed right away was the addition of Tailscale to the share sheet on Android and iOS, which meant I could quickly share photos and other files between all my devices in seconds (no AirDrop or Android Quick Share required). I could also instantly access the shared folders on my desktop and laptop computers from my phone.

Something else you can do very easily is set up a remote access app on a phone and use it to connect directly to one of your computers in a different physical location, with no exposure to the wider internet and no advanced configuration required—Tailscale provides you with an IP address that looks like a local network. Any of your home computers can be configured as an exit node as well, which means internet traffic can be rerouted through it. If you're in a hotel, for example, you can use Tailscale as a secure tunnel back home, which means websites see you as visiting from home rather than an unrecognized hotel IP address.

There are some areas where Tailscale can improve (the Windows client isn't quite as straightforward to use as the macOS one), and it's fair to say at least some basic networking knowledge is required to get to grips with Tailscale, but in terms of software that's free and useful, it's hard to beat. I didn't dive into more advanced use cases involving NAS drives or home servers, as they're not something that I'm working with at the moment, but that's the next level of Tailscale capability

title: These Are the Best Smart Home Gifts of 2026
description: If someone on your list wants to make their home a bit smarter, check these gifts out.
fullText:
If someone on your gift list is looking to make their home smarter, the challenge can be daunting. There are a lot of smart products out there, all with varying price points and feature sets. What's more, smart home designs can be as simple or as complex as the user wants them to be: Maybe someone wants to be able to control their lights with the same convenient smart speaker they use to listen to music, while others might want their house running on automations.

If you're here, you likely know your giftee is looking for smart home devices but aren't sure where to start. As such, I've compiled some of the most popular smart categories and highlighted a specific product that is generally best for the majority of users interested in that type of device. (Though, with all technology gifts, my main piece of advice is asking what your recipient wants exactly—that will help eliminate risks of buying something incompatible with their systems, or something that requires a subscription they don't want to pay for.)

"Smart home" encompasses a myriad of product categories, but for me, the most important is arguably the smart speaker. It's the most universal by far: A smart speaker can act as a smart hub to power the rest of your smart home, or it can be your only smart device. Maybe someone on your list wants to build out their smart home, and this is their first step, or they simply want something that can play music and tell them the weather at the same time.

It's tough to pick a smart speaker to recommend over all others, since this category is particularly platform-dependent. If your giftee is all-in on the Apple ecosystem, the HomePod mini could be the best choice; on the other hand, if they love Google products, the Google Home Speaker could be equally as solid. However, if I have to choose one speaker over all others, I'd have to go with Amazon. It's not that I necessarily think Amazon's product has the best audio quality, but I do think it's the most universal speaker of the bunch. It doesn't matter what platform your recipient depends on; they can connect their Amazon speaker to it and power any number of smart home devices. If they happen to have other Amazon devices, like a Fire TV or Kindle, even better; if not, it won't hurt.

Amazon makes quite a few smart speakers these days, but I'm focused on the best bang for your buck here. For that, the Echo Dot Max might take the cake. It's a bit more powerful than the Echo Dot, with more audio tech (Amazon says it has a tweeter and woofer, compared to the single front-firing speaker of the Dot), plus it's a more recent device (2025 vs. 2022). While you could upgrade to the Echo Studio, which has better audio tech than the Dot Max, the former costs nearly double. The Echo Dot Max seems to be the better overall value—or, you could gift someone two Echo Dot Max for a stereo setup, for the price of one Echo Studio.

Other than smart speakers, smart lights are probably the first device that comes to mind when I think "smart home." Not only are they easy to set up and use, but they're perhaps the easiest demonstration of how your smart home works: Most people get a kick out of turning lights on and off with voice commands, as well as changing the colors on a whim.

There are a ton of smart lights to choose from on the market, with varying brands, price points, and features to consider. But if you want to get someone started with a set of smart lights, WiZ might have the best value. These smart lights run just over $20 per bulb, but drop in individual price quickly when you buy in multi-packs. A two-pack is $21.99, a three-pack is $24.99, and a four-pack is $37.99. These WiZ bulbs are CNET's pick for best smart lights of 2026, in part because of the affordable price, but also because they don't require a hub, support a wide range of platforms, and come with both color-changing and motion-sensing capabilities.

If you google "best smart cameras of 2026," you're going to find a host of brands and opinions out there. Ring, Blink, Arlo, Google, and more top all of the best-of lists out there, with features like pan and tilt, 4K video, AI capabilities, cloud video storage, etc. The problem is, many of the best smart camera features require a subscription, which I'm not a huge fan of for gifts. You want someone to be able to use the thing you buy them without also having to worry about a monthly or annual payment. And unless you're willing to keep that subscription going for them, you might want to find an option that works well without one.

That's why I'd lean towards the Eufy EufyCam C35. Eufy's outdoor camera is reasonably priced, especially when it's on sale (currently $54.99). It comes with two-way audio, as well as color night vision, and it supports on-device media storage. CNET recommends adding an SD card or Eufy hub for expanded local storage, and even a solar panel if you want to avoid having to recharge the camera every now and again. The video resolution here isn't as sharp as some other models, capping at 1080p, but that means less video data to worry about. Plus, the whole operation works without a subscription. If you're looking for something with more features, CNET has an excellent list of the best smart cameras of 2026.

If someone in your life is looking for a smart lock, prepare yourself: These things can get a bit pricey. I suppose that's to be expected. If you're going to trust a piece of tech to keep your front door protected, you want it to be good at its job, which means it might tend to cost more than other individual smart home devices.

For the money, one of the best and most feature-rich smart locks you can buy is Yale's Assure Lock 2. It isn't the cheapest smart lock on the market, but it's not the priciest. For that price ($240), you get a versatile smart lock that works with all the major platforms (Alexa, Google, and Apple Home), supports digital passes, key-free unlocking, app control, and comes with a simple keypad for easy unlocking. There's even a version that comes with a fingerprint reader if your giftee is looking for a smart lock with biometrics, but that will up the price a bit more.

Now, other smart locks tend to hover around this price point, if not even higher. But if you're looking for something that isn't quite as expensive without compromising the feature list too much, check out the Ultraloq U-Bolt Pro. CNET highlights this option as a more affordable smart lock (around $110) that has keypad and fingerprint entry, as well as IP65 weather resistance. However, the big trade-off is the lack of Apple support, so if you're all in on Siri, you'll need to look elsewhere.

Like smart locks, smart doorbells can get expensive fast. And like smart locks, that's for a good reason. You want your video doorbell to catch everything, whether that's a delivery made while you're away or an intruder looking for ways to break in.

For most people looking for a smart video doorbell, the best choice might just be the TP-Link Tapo D225. It's reasonably priced and comes with 2K video with a wide 180-degree angle, with both wired and wireless installation options. If your giftee doesn't feel like hard-wiring the doorbell to their house, they can get by on eight months of battery life in between charges. It also supports a number of platforms, including Alexa, Google Home, and IFTTT, though unfortunately not Apple Home. They'll also need to provide their own SD card for footage, or pay for cloud storage.

If you need an alternative, Arlo's second-generation video doorbell is also excellent, and is PCMag's pick for best smart doorbell. This option is around the same price, is easy to set up, has excellent video quality with a wide-angle view, and runs on a charge for four months at a time (though you can also hard-wire the doorbell if you wish). Arlo also doesn't support Apple Home, but it does support a wide variety of other platforms, including Alexa, Google Home, IFTTT, and Samsung SmartThings.

The big caveat here is that you will need an Arlo Secure subscription in order to access certain features. That includes motion alerts, notifications, and even recorded video, which can be a bummer if your giftee isn't interested in a subscription. As such, I'd point most toward the TP-Link option.

Here's what I look for in a smart security camera: high-quality video, night vision support, and smart motion detection, all without requiring a subscription for many (or any) of the features. (Bonus points if there's a built-in spotlight.)

Speaking of TP-Link in the last category, I'd also recommend the company if you're looking for a smart home camera. Specifically, the TP-Link Tapo Wire-Free MagCam. This smart camera supports 2K video, color night vision, both local and cloud-based video recording, with an extended battery life running up to almost a year. Those perks, combined with its reasonable price, make it a great choice for a smart camera gift, and are why PCMag named it the best 2K wireless camera of the year. I particularly like that you don't need a subscription for any of these features, so your recipient can simply set up the camera and get monitoring.

Again, TP-Link doesn't support Apple Home, but it does support Alexa, Google Assistant, and IFTTT. It also doesn't have a mechanical pan and tilt system, so it won't be able to move to capture more of your yard. If your giftee is looking for something that supports this type of security capture, PCMag recommends Arlo Essential Outdoor Pan Tilt. This one's even less expensive than the Tapo C310, and also supports 2K video. That said, it requires payment to access recorded video and receive AI-powered alerts, and you have to use Arlo's cloud-based recording solution, as there is no local recording here. For those reasons, I'd recommend the TP-Link for more users.

title: How to Get the Most Cloud Storage Possible for Free
description: You can get a decent amount of storage without paying a dime.
fullText:
Cloud storage is likely an essential part of your data management strategy, whether you're just using Google Drive for documents or you back up everything to a remote service. You can get a significant amount of space for a reasonable monthly fee, but if you prefer not to pay, it's possible to combine free options and cobble together quite a bit of free storage—around 80GB (or more)—at no cost.

A reminder: You shouldn't rely solely on cloud storage for your backups. Follow the 3-2-1 rule, which protects against a single point of failure, such as getting locked out of your account or issues with the service itself.

The most obvious option for free storage is Google Drive. Google offers up to 15GB of storage per account, though this is split across all Google apps, including Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos as well as Android backups. You could create multiple Google accounts, which would allow you to stack 15GB allotments. Note that Google recently introduced a 5GB free storage cap on some new accounts, though you can get around this by linking a phone number.

iCloud users automatically get 5GB of free storage, split across backups, photos, and files, as well as data from Messages, Mail, Contacts, FaceTime, voice memos, and Apple Invites. You can delete content to reduce the size of your iCloud backup to manage available storage space. The cheapest paid iCloud+ tier comes with 50GB storage for around $1 per month.

Similar to iCloud, OneDrive comes with 5GB of free cloud storage, and all you need is a Microsoft 365 account. This limit is shared across documents, files, and photos—Outlook gets a separate 15GB allotment.

Box offers 10GB of secure storage on its free plan. There's a 250GB file upload limit, so this isn't the best option for media or larger files, plus you only get access to one file version. Free users do get 5 e-signature requests per month, so Box is a good choice for documents.

Dropbox's free plan is limited to just 2GB of storage, which can be filled with photos, documents, and files from up to three devices. You can also use Dropbox to share files and collaborate with other users, and the service integrates with many third-party apps.

Proton is known for its privacy-focused products, so Proton Drive is a good choice for storing sensitive records like tax returns and legal documents. The free plan comes with 5GB of space, and your vault is end-to-end encrypted.

MEGA allows a whopping 20GB of storage to free users with automatic backups and 100 file versions, making it a solid option for large archives and media.

There are a handful of other cloud storage providers that offer free plans without aggressive ads, major file size limitations, or serious privacy compromises. Other options include Sync.com (5GB), Icedrive (10GB), and pCloud (up to 10GB), though some users on Reddit have noted reliability and customer support concerns with these services.

Your password manager subscription may not technically be free, but if you're already paying for it, you may have some small amount of secure file storage at no additional cost. Bitwarden's Premium plan comes with 5 GB of encrypted storage, while many others (1Password, Proton Pass, and Dashlane, to name a few) include 1 GB.

If you are using multiple cloud storage services, you can distribute different content types across each to maximize features and ease of access. Proton Drive and Sync.com are good choices for sensitive files you want to be sure are secure, though you can use a tool like Cryptomator (which is free and open source) to encrypt your vault before syncing to a service like Google Drive or Box.

Google Drive, OneDrive, and iCloud are best for files and documents you need regularly, including items that require collaboration and sharing, as well as device backups. MEGA could be a solid option for cold storage—media that doesn't change or need to be accessed often. And Box is useful for smaller documents, like PDF records and receipts, given its individual file size limit.

title: 10 Hacks Every macOS 27 User Should Know
description: You can create your own Safari extensions using AI.
fullText:
macOS 27 Golden Gate is now available for every Mac that runs Apple Silicon. As long as you don't own a Mac with an Intel processor, you should be able to update to macOS 27. This update includes a bunch of new features, but Apple's focus has been more on stability, bug fixes, and to some extent, fixing some design missteps from macOS 26. I've been running Golden Gate on my primary Mac for a few weeks now, and these are the 10 best macOS 27 hacks I've found:

macOS 26 Tahoe introduced Liquid Glass animations, but that didn't resonate with many users. Apple has walked back those changes since, and with macOS 27, you can use a slider to precisely control Liquid Glass effects. I think reducing Liquid Glass improves readability, so that's what I've chosen. To make the change, click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your Mac's display, and select System Settings > Appearance. You can now use the slider in the "Liquid Glass" section. Move it to the right to reduce the effect.

Pull-to-refresh, developed by former Apple engineer Loren Brichter, is one of the iPhone's most iconic gestures. This gesture has now arrived on the Mac, as some first-party apps now let you pull-to-refresh in macOS 27. You can try it on your MacBook (or iMac if you have a trackpad) by opening a webpage in Safari, and performing a two-finger swipe gesture. If you use natural scrolling, then you can use two fingers to swipe downwards. If not, then swipe upwards with two fingers. This will refresh the webpage. The gesture also works in Mail, Calendar, News, and Podcasts

There's a new drawing tool in Apple Notes and Freeform in macOS 27, which you can use to create art and other drawings. To try it in Freeform, open the app, and click the pen icon in the toolbar up top. You can now use the trackpad or a mouse to draw on the board. Similarly, you can select a note (or create a new one) in Apple Notes, hit the pen icon, and start sketching.

macOS 27 has a dedicated Siri app, which you can use for all interactions with the virtual assistant. Once you open the app, you can speak or type your request, and Siri will handle the rest. If you disable "Hey Siri," as I've done, opening the Siri app automatically shows a "Type to Siri" popover. You can then type your request, which I've been using to set timers and reminders. The Siri app can also answer your questions, and handle all the tasks that the virtual assistant used to do before macOS 27.

If you've enabled Apple Intelligence on your Mac, you can use "Visual Intelligence" to learn more about things on your screen. To use it, go to System Settings > Siri, and ensure that Siri AI is enabled. Next, press Command-Shift-6, and select an area of your screen. Siri AI will analyze the image and show you these options: You can use the "Ask Siri" text box to find specific information about the image. Or, click "Image Search" to check the internet for other copies of the object or photo. Depending on what Siri AI finds in the image, you may see other options such as adding a phone number to contacts, or viewing an address in Apple Maps.

When you AirPlay to your Mac from another Apple device, the video takes up the entire screen. I prefer it if AirPlay opens in a window, as opposed to full-screen mode. In macOS 27, you can set this up via a Terminal command, as discovered by the user pdfu from MacRumors Forums. Use this command in Terminal:

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain && \ sudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/ControlCenter APReceiverInWindow -dict Enabled -bool true

Now, restart your Mac. The next time you AirPlay from another device to your Mac, you'll notice that the video opens in a resizable window. To restore default settings, use this command in Terminal, and restart your Mac after:

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/ControlCenter APReceiverInWindow

Safari in macOS 27 allows you to automatically organize related tabs. This feature is enabled by default, but I don't like how it starts grouping tabs on its own. Instead, I prefer to receive Safari's tab grouping suggestions and to group them myself. This is because I've found automatic tab organization sometimes misses a tab or two. Open Safari in macOS 27, and click the Safari menu at the top of the page. Go to Settings > Tabs, and click the drop-down menu next to "Organize tabs." Select "Show Related Tabs," and you're good to go.

Once you have Siri AI enabled, you can use "Describe Extension." This feature uses AI to create Safari extensions for you, and all you have to do is type what you're looking for. To try it out, open Safari on your Mac, load any website, and click the three-line button in the address bar. Here, select Describe Extension. You'll see a pop-up with a text box, and some helpful prompts to get you started. You can make something as simple as an extension that automatically closes duplicate tabs, or more complex tasks such as changing the stylesheet of a website to add some holiday cheer to each page.

Siri AI is helpful in macOS 27, but it also appears everywhere. I find it particularly annoying when I see the Siri AI button every time I right-click anywhere on my MacBook. Thankfully, there's an easy way to remove it from the context menu, which I discovered on Reddit. Use the following Terminal command, and then restart your Mac:

codes=(soft apwn exit loca lock logo rlgo rcnt rrst rest rsdn shut slep spro syss) args=(-int 0) for code in $codes; do hex=$(printf %s "$code" | xxd -p -u) args+=(-int "$((16#$hex))") done defaults write -g NSAppleMenuAllowedItems -array "${args[@]}"

To restore default settings, use this command:

defaults delete -g NSAppleMenuAllowedItems

If you prefer keyboard navigation, you'll know you can use the arrow keys to switch between different menus at the top of your Mac's screen. Once you select a menu item in any app, you can press the right arrow key to go to the next menu, eg: going from "File" to "Edit." The left arrow key takes you to the previous menu item, however, this navigation stops with the last menu item, which is usually "Help." In macOS 27, there's a hidden feature that allows you to switch from the last app menu item to the first menu bar app using your arrow keys. You'll have to enable this using Terminal, and restart your Mac for it to take effect. Use this Terminal command to enable the feature:

defaults write -g NSMenuEnableMenuBarAgent -bool true
defaults write -g NSMenuBarUseAgentNavigation -bool true

To disable the feature, use this command:

defaults delete -g NSMenuEnableMenuBarAgent
defaults delete -g NSMenuBarUseAgentNavigation

title: The key talking points from Pocognoli's bold Scotland squad
description: The Sebastien Pocognoli Scotland era is already creating serious intrigue - and the Belgian's squad are yet to assemble for a training-ground rondo, never mind play a game.
fullText:
Six new call-ups, seven uncapped players, a refreshed defence, a more-of-the-same midfield and an exciting, new-look attack.

The Sebastien Pocognoli Scotland era is already creating serious intrigue - and the Belgian's squad are yet to assemble for a training-ground rondo, never mind play a game.

The 39-year-old's first taste of competitive action starts with a Nations League opener in Slovenia on 26 September - live on the BBC - beginning an extended four-game international period.

In the meantime, let's dissect the talking points from a bold 28-man selection.

McBurnie & seven uncapped players in Scotland squad

Scotland fans allowed to buy alcohol at upcoming games

Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack?

There have been no new call-ups in the goalkeeping department. Angus Gunn, now playing with San Jose Earthquakes in the MLS, has 25 caps and will be the favourite to continue between the sticks.

Pocognoli's first selection has shown that a surprise is not beyond him, though. The Belgian stressed the importance of his style in relation to his squad picks, and Falkirk's Scott Bain is a goalkeeper who can deal with the ball at his feet.

Jon McCracken is also playing regularly for Bradford City in England's League One, but Liam Kelly very much remains second choice at Rangers.

As for the backline, the new Scotland boss has predominantly played with a back three throughout his coaching career at both Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco.

He insists on his teams being aggressive in and out of possession, so will want defenders capable of picking brave passes but also with the pace to cover big distances when playing a high line.

Scott McKenna, Jack Hendry and Kieran Tierney all have experience of playing in a back three under Steve Clarke, albeit the approach will differ under Pocognoli. Captain Andy Robertson also clocked up a lot of minutes at left wing-back.

Aaron Hickey, Nathan Patterson and young Colby Donovan, who has impressed Pocognoli "but needs to improve on things like every young lad", are options for the opposite flank.

Uncapped trio Luis Binks, Stephen Welsh and Luke Graham add more depth at centre-back.

Brondby captain Binks, who qualifies for Scotland through a grandparent, has had an interesting career. "The feeling and the timing about him was right," Pocognoli said of the former Bologna and Como man.

At the age of 25, the left-footed centre-back has already played in the MLS, Serie A, English Championship and now Denmark's top tier.

Meanwhile, Stoke's Graham - also left-footed - enjoyed a breakthrough spell at Dundee last season and continues to excel in England's second division, along with Swansea's Welsh, who proved he could thrive in a possession-based Motherwell side last term.

It is much of the same in midfield, although Scott McTominay is absent following a successful heart procedure and Udinese's Lennon Miller is back after being left out of Clarke's World Cup squad.

There is a welcome return for McTominay's Napoli team-mate Billy Gilmour, who suffered a crushing injury just before the start of the finals.

Arguably Scotland's most composed midfielder and best progressive passer, many expect the 25-year-old to thrive in Pocognoli's system. Miller, 20, could also fall into that category.

Experienced campaigners John McGinn, Ryan Christie, Kenny McLean and Lewis Ferguson - the Scots' standout performer earlier this summer - are all included in a seven-man midfield selection, which also features thriving Hearts player Josh McPake.

Signed this summer from St Johnstone, it has been a remarkable rise for the 24-year-old, who has been listed as a midfielder in the squad despite featuring on the left wing for the Tynecastle side. He was a Stirling Albion player just two years ago.

While Ben Gannon-Doak, Findlay Curtis and McPake offer options in attacking wide areas, there is a centre-forward spot up for grabs in the absence of injured pair Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, plus the omission of Lyndon Dykes.

A free-scoring spell in Sweden earned Robbie Ure the number nine shirt at Sevilla, Oli McBurnie and his Hull team have made an impressive return to the Premier League and Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie scored in a win against Juventus on Sunday.

"Players who are performing well are in the new pathway," Pocognoli said when asked about Rangers academy product Ure, who is yet to score since his switch to La Liga.

"Robbie is adapting well to La Liga. He's put in some good performances, but he maybe needs to adapt to the intensity. Being selected gives him an opportunity."

On the return of McBurnie, who has received his first Scotland call-up in five years, he added: "It's regarding style of play, playing time and performance. I have to start on a new journey, a new book and it's a new opportunity for some players."

The head coach also spoke of his desire to mix youth with the "DNA and heritage" of his squad, evidenced by the inclusion of teenage James Wilson, who is showing signs of fulfilling his serious potential at Hearts.

title: PGA Tour not planning return programme for LIV stars
description: PGA Tour chief executive Brian Rolapp says there are no plans to create an instant pathway back for LIV Golf's biggest stars after the breakaway series filed for bankruptcy protection.
fullText:
There are no plans to create an instant pathway back to the PGA Tour for LIV Golf's biggest stars.

Major winners Jon Rahm, Bryson DeChambeau and Cameron Smith are contemplating their futures after LIV filed for bankruptcy protection last week as the breakaway league tries to create a new circuit for next year.

Rahm said he was uncertain about his future plans.

"There's a long legal process they have to go through before a lot of things fall into place," the Spaniard said before playing this week's BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.

"I really can't give you an answer right now."

The PGA Tour is pressing ahead with its plans for a revamped set-up in 2028 but chief executive Brian Rolapp offered no guarantees that LIV's biggest names will be welcomed back.

"In terms of where we are today, we are not currently contemplating a returning member programme like the one you saw in January," Rolapp said.

Brooks Koepka took a deal that brought him back to the US tour at the start of the year but the arrangement was rejected by DeChambeau, Rahm and Smith.

LIV files for bankruptcy protection with over $45m owed to players

What next for LIV Golf's star players, and its fight for survival?

If players abandon LIV, it was thought their most likely route back to the PGA Tour would be through playing the DP World Tour.

Currently, the leading 10 finishers on the Race to Dubai earn cards for the American circuit, but that may change.

Rolapp admitted no deal has been struck over how many DP World Tour players will qualify for his circuit when it splits into a promotion and relegation setup with Championship and Challenger tiers from 2028.

Golfers who defected to LIV were hit with one-year bans that could be served while playing on the DP World Tour. Now it seems there are no guarantees as the revamping of the game's leading circuit continues.

"The PGA Tour is built on meritocracy," Rolapp said. "Every player, whether they are a member or want to become one, must earn their place.

"We are a membership organisation; we have rules, and those rules exist for lots of reasons, including fairness and competitive balance. Rules matter, and they must be enforced."

Rolapp added: "Accountability and discipline, these are essential elements for any sports league and are certainly for the integrity of the PGA Tour and the sport. It's what holds the tour together.

"Those are guiding principles for us."

Negotiations with the DP World Tour over how many players will progress from the European based organisation to the PGA Tour are still to be concluded and the number of cards could be reduced.

"That's very much under discussion both internally and as we continue our discussions with the DP World Tour," Rolapp said.

"The spirit of those conversations are very productive. Both sides are trying to think creatively about how we modify and improve the relationship we have.

"Like any discussions, there's things we agree on, things we don't agree on, things we're trying to work through, and we'll continue to do that."

Rory McIIroy says he is not worried that a deal with the DP World Tour has yet to be concluded, but he warned that cards being made available for the lower Challenger Series would be less attractive.

"I don't see any reason why a DP World Tour player would go to the Challenger Series," said the two-time Masters champion. "I don't see that as an upward move in your career. I see it as a very lateral move."

McIlroy added: "No one's going to argue that the Championship Series is going to be the highest level of tour golf that you can play, and then it's just deciding what an adequate number of cards is to go from here to the Championship Series."

title: How Kenya won its bid for 2029 World Athletics Championships
description: Kenya's athletics-loving population and improved infrastructure helped Nairobi secure the rights to host the 2029 World Championships, but challenges remain to ensure a successful event.
fullText:
Kenya's President William Ruto says the World Athletics Championship will be "coming home", with Nairobi set to make history after being selected as the first African city to host the event in 2029.

Ruto hailed the winning bid as a "victory for generations of athletes" who have made the nation "synonymous with excellence" on the track and road.

Nairobi beat London and Rome to the hosting rights, with Munich selected to stage the 2031 edition.

After missing out on the 2025 World Championships to Tokyo, a series of factors helped Kenya see off its European rivals this time around.

When World Athletics president Lord Coe announced the decision in Budapest on Tuesday, he described Kenya's bid as "compelling and emotional".

The East African nation is the second-most successful nation in the history of the World Championships with 72 gold medals, placing it behind the United States.

The vast majority of those glories, alongside 38 Olympic gold medals, have come in middle- and long-distance running.

Lord Coe said that athletics is "woven into the fabric" of the nation and that Kenyans have helped "shape the history" of the sport.

He name-checked several runners including two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge - who was involved in the lobbying for Kenya's bid - men's 800m world record holder David Rudisha and multiple world and Olympic medallist Faith Kipyegon.

A passionate fanbase is also one of the country's great strengths.

Some 68% of Kenyans surveyed by World Athletics rated their interest in athletics as high, compared with a global average of 39%.

Athletics is the country's second-most followed sport, behind only football, and when World Athletics assessed its social media channels, Kenya was the fourth-highest nation in terms of followers.

Kenya's previous bid for the 2025 edition fell down largely on the facilities which the country possessed.

This time around, the Kasarani Stadium will have gone through a complete structural upgrade well before the world's top athletes descend on Nairobi.

The 48,000-capacity venue will be used when Kenya co-hosts football's 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) next June and July alongside Tanzania and Uganda.

"We learned from the 2025 bid because there were areas that we did not score well," Barnaba Korir, who worked on the successful bid, told the BBC World Service.

"Because of that, we managed to improve on those areas.

"I'm happy that the infrastructure that we have already developed will also meet the standards that we have seen all over the world."

Hotel space is one area not expected to be a problem, with Nairobi a regular host for large conventions.

"Kenya is also known for its very dynamic hospitality, the tourism sector," Elijah Mwangi, principal secretary at the State Department for Sports, told the BBC.

"It has a game park within the city, so we are waiting to welcome everybody."

President Ruto made financial and security guarantees in order to secure the Championships.

"We thank World Athletics for the confidence it has placed in Kenya," Ruto said.

"We will honour that confidence by delivering an unforgettable championship worthy of our athletes, our country and our continent."

Lord Coe became president of World Athletics (then known as the IAAF) in 2015 and has pledged to grow the sport around the globe.

During his time in office the World Championships have been hosted in Qatar (2019), the United States (2022) and Tokyo, while China's capital Beijing will stage them in 2027.

Kenya has successfully hosted age-grade events in Nairobi and the World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, while the World Athletics Relays were held in Botswana's capital Gaborone in May.

With Coe's third term in office coming to an end next year, one official involved in Kenya's bid, speaking before the host announcement, said it was "unthinkable" that Nairobi would not succeed.

"With this decision we continue to fulfil our mission of growing athletics worldwide," Coe said.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances.

Coe hailed the "quality, ambition and commitment" of all four bidding cities.

London, Munich and Rome have all previously held the Olympics, with the World Championships in London as recently as 2017, but the chance to break new ground in Africa was clearly compelling.

UK Athletics chief executive Jack Buckner said his team was "deeply disappointed" to see London miss out.

Kenya now faces logistical and organisational challenges over the next three years as it prepares to deliver Africa's first World Championships.

With the 2027 Afcon looming large on the horizon, Nairobi will have a chance to test-run getting fans in and out of the Kasarani Stadium, which lies about a half-hour drive from the city's central business district.

The venue does not have any rail connections but Korir says World Athletics officials were "very satisfied" by Kenya's transport plan.

There were instances of overcrowding when the stadium hosted Kenya games at football's African Nations Championships last year, which led to the capacity being reduced for some matches.

Delays in preparations for Afcon have raised concerns, and the funding for the World Championships will come entirely from the Kenyan government.

Mwangi revealed that $78m (£58.5m) is the current estimate for the government's contribution, with sponsorship deals also playing a role.

"We are prepared to ensure that whatever is expected to be paid, it is paid in the due time," he added.

Presidential elections are scheduled for next year, but Korir is confident organisers will secure the "huge" and "legally binding" figure earmarked even if there is a change in government.

"Whatever the government assigns now will be observed by the next government. It is an international agreement," he said.

Then comes ticketing, first to make sure the local population are not priced out and then to ensure the stands are filled.

The cheapest tickets for the Under-18 World Championships in 2017 were priced at 200 Kenyan shillings ($1.15, £1.14) but attendances were low until entry was made free.

World Athletics generated $522m in revenue from Tokyo 2025, with a total of 619,000 tickets sold over the nine days of competition, while London sold a record 705,000 tickets in 2017.

In passing up the opportunity of returning to the British capital, World Athletics has chosen expansion over guaranteed ticket sales, but attendances will be scrutinised - especially after the sparse numbers seen in the stands in Doha in 2019.

Korir, however, is confident the Kasarani Stadium "will be full" on "every day" of competition, including morning sessions, if sales begin early enough.

Meanwhile, Kenya has endured a spate of doping scandals in recent years, with 11 individuals banned by the Athletics Integrity Unit so far this year alone.

The pressure is now on the East African nation to deliver on its promises in the build-up to Nairobi 2029 and ensure the Championships pass off without any major issues.

Additional reporting by Ian Williams and Celestine Karoney.

title: Sterling admits dangerous driving on motorway before crash
description: The former England winger crashed a Lamborghini into motorway barriers in May.
fullText:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before he crashed a Lamborghini in May.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

Sterling, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of 28 May.

Sterling has 82 England caps, the last of which was won at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

The former England winger pleaded guilty to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road before he crashed.

The court heard he strayed into the central reservation of the M3, exited at junction 4A, and veered off the A327, crashing into "roadside infrastructure" in a layby.

The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

He was in possession of six canisters of nitrous oxide, a Class C drug.

Prosecutor Simon Jones said that between 7:45 and 8:52 police received a number of calls about dangerous driving on the two motorways.

When police arrived on the scene of the collision Sterling was in the passenger seat of the car with two nitrous oxide canisters on his lap, the court was told.

Witnesses described seeing a Lamborghini driver inhaling from a white balloon.

Fiona Jennings, who saw the vehicle on the M3 at 8:45, said she looked across and thought that an airbag had inflated, but then realised it was an inflated balloon.

She told police she saw "absolutely horrendous driving" as the Lamborghini swerved in and out of lanes.

"She had genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," Jones said.

Sterling complied with a road side breath test, which was negative, and a preliminary drug test, which indicated no cannabis or cocaine.

However, tests carried out at the Basingstoke police investigation centre deemed that he was impaired.

During the process he disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", Jones said.

A sample of blood could only be taken with his consent, which he did not give.

Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision, Mr Jones said, but in the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer".

In the police interview that followed, Sterling accepted he had been the driver, and provided "no comment" answers to the driving.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that the case was a "top category" because of the "at times" serious impairment, though it would have been for short periods within the driving.

But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious, and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

Hampshire Police previously said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision near the M3 southbound, near the Minley interchange.

The force said no other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.

Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands.

In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022.

With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015.

He is currently without a club.

In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.

Sterling, who was seen listening attentively in the dock, was granted unconditional bail.

District Judge Kirsty Allman ordered a pre-sentence report to be carried out before the next hearing, where she will determine whether to sentence at the magistrates' court or send it to crown court.

Sterling will next appear in court on 25 November, and has been disqualified from driving in the interim.

title: Tuchel regrets not eating Azteca turf after win over Mexico
description: Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's epic World Cup win against Mexico.
fullText:
Thomas Tuchel regrets not eating any of the grass at the Azteca Stadium after England's World Cup win against Mexico.

His Three Lions beat the co-hosts 3-2 in the last-16 tie in July, despite playing much of the second half with 10 men following Jarell Quansah's red card.

England went on to reach the semi-finals, where they lost to Argentina, before beating France in the Bronze medal match for third place.

Tuchel, though, made a bizarre admission during an interview with Daniel Sturridge for the FA's forthcoming feature 'Reflections: England's World Cup Journey'.

He said: "I texted a friend after the match and I just wrote, 'I regret that I didn't eat some grass after the match to keep something from this in my body forever'. That was the feeling. That was the moment.

England's victory was only the third time Mexico had tasted defeat at the stadium in 90 competitive matches.

Tuchel described it as one of the highlights of the campaign and hailed the "huge bond" within the camp, especially the reaction to Jordan Henderson's tournament-ending injury after falling over an advertising hoarding while celebrating the Azteca success.

"This game had so much of what you could wish for," added the German. "If you needed any proof of what it meant to these players and how they were with each other, it was the moment Jordan fell over and broke his arm.

"Within a second, the players were there. Every single player was there stopping the celebrations, building a shield, protecting Jordan, not going anywhere, in full empathy. It was so special."

England are next in action against World Cup winners Spain on 26 September in their 2026-27 Uefa Nations League opener, with the 2028 European Championships also on Tuchel's radar.

Confident of ending England's wait for a first senior men's trophy since 1966, he believed their World Cup run not only cemented his relationship with the squad - "it feels like they are my players now" - but also represented "something to build on".

Tuchel added: "I'm very excited. I think we got another step closer and I think we're there."

title: VAR did not even consider if Fernandez was offside - Webb
description: Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) did not even consider whether Enzo Fernandez was offside for Erling Haaland's controversial winner in Sunday's Manchester derby.
fullText:
Referees' chief Howard Webb has admitted that the video assistant referee (VAR) did not even consider whether Enzo Fernandez was offside for Erling Haaland's controversial winner in Sunday's Manchester derby.

Speaking on the first edition of 'Match Officials Mic'd Up' of the season, Webb said he was "really disappointed" with the error made by the VAR Matt Donohue and his assistant Blake Antrobus.

Manchester City striker Haaland thought he had scored the only goal of the game at Old Trafford in the 60th minute, but it was disallowed on the field for offside.

A VAR review found Haaland was just onside, and the goal was awarded.

But it immediately became apparent that the video officials had made an error in failing to identify an offside offence by Fernandez, diving at the ball in a central position and interfering with opponents.

"I was really disappointed with this outcome. We all are," said Webb, Premier League refereeing body Pro Ref's chief refereeing officer.

"None more so than the officials themselves. They take a lot of personal pride in what they do and they're obviously hurting now, having fallen short in this situation.

"They'll not be officiating again until after the international break."

One of the questions which many supporters have asked is how the VAR team could possibly reach the conclusion that Fernandez did not commit an offside offence.

Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez initially appeared to be marking Haaland, but then moved over to try and intercept the ball from Fernandez. This left Haaland free at the back post to finish.

Former England striker and BBC Sport pundit Wayne Rooney said on Match of the Day that "to not see that and recognise that Enzo Fernandez was in an offside position...anyone who has played the game at any level understands that and to get it so wrong is baffling."

The Mic'd Up audio revealed that at no stage did Donohue or Antrobus consider whether Fernandez was offside because, as Webb describes, they got "tunnel vision" over Haaland.

The semi-automated offside technology told the VAR that Haaland was three centimetres onside from Josko Gvardiol's cross.

But the video officials then only checked for a touch by Fernandez which would have created a new offside phase against the Norway international.

This is the transcript, which was dominated by the VAR with the AVAR only making one minor contribution.

At the start of the season, video officials were encouraged to be more efficient with their checks and not take an excessive amount of time.

Comments made by the technical replay operator have been omitted.

VAR: Checking the on-field decision of offside against Haaland.

The VAR and the semi-automated offside operator then discuss the decision against Haaland and he is shown to be onside.

VAR: Okay, so he's onside. So we now need to check the full APP (attacking phase).

VAR speaking to referee Michael Oliver: Michael, Haaland's in an onside position, but I need to check the full APP now. Stand by.

VAR: Haaland's clearly onside. Roll it all the way through. Roll it all the way through.

VAR: Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go.

VAR: Go back just to check Ndiaye wasn't on offside. Sorry, my apologies. When it's flicked. Quick, quick, quick, quick. Yes, fine. Go, go, go, go, go.

VAR: Let's go. It should be a goal. All the way into the back of the net now.

VAR: Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!

This is the point at which Gvardiol crosses the ball into the box.

VAR: Deflection. Onside. No touch there [by Fernandez]. Confirm, no touch. There wasn't.

VAR: Just something [camera angle] tighter. Clear gap.

VAR: There's not a touch, is there [by Fernandez]? There's no touch.

VAR: Another angle. Roll it through, roll it through, roll it through.

VAR to referee: Michael, confirming that you need to change your decision to goal. Haaland is in onside position. Final decision is goal. Check complete.

Webb said that the VAR failed to assess how Fernandez found himself in that position, so did not consider the offside offence.

"The VAR gets super-focused on Haaland," said Webb, who had already been in contact with Manchester United to share the VAR audio and video.

"He establishes he's onside, he thinks that's a good goal.

"He doesn't truly evaluate the full impact of Fernandez's position. He has a look to see if he touches the ball, because then that relates to potentially knocking it to Haaland, who goes on to score."

Webb highlighted the lack of assistance from Antrobus as the assistant VAR, who did not offer a meaningful contribution during the review.

"In that moment, he [Donohue] gets tunnel vision," Webb said. "It's down to the rest of his team to pull him out of that tunnel, and unfortunately, that didn't happen on this occasion.

"What looks like a really clear subjective offside, because Fernandez doesn't touch the ball but still clearly impacts [the play but] doesn't get identified, and it's really disappointing.

"This goal should've been disallowed. And highly unfortunately, it wasn't, and we'll review it, reflect upon it, and try to take the learning forward to prevent this unusual type of error from happening again."

There was also much debate over the red card shown to Phil Foden in the 23th minute for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes, largely because there was no sanction against the Portuguese midfielder for a similar act.

Webb backed the decision to dismiss Foden, but said the action by Fernandes did not meet the threshold for violent conduct.

"I agree with the red card for Phil Foden," said Webb. "He kicks out with force into the upper body of Bruno Fernandes.

"Now, when you look at the footage, there is that petulant kick by Bruno Fernandes into the backside of Foden. It is more petulant than violent.

"To be violent conduct, it has to have excessive force or brutality. When you look at that, particularly in full speed, it doesn't have those elements. So therefore, this would be a yellow card offence."

Webb added that if Foden had not been sent off on the field, but he had been via a VAR review - as Aston Villa's Joao Gomes was at Brighton for a similar offence last month - Fernandes' yellow-card offence would also have been identified at the pitchside monitor.

title: Cisco email security boxes can be rooted by an email
description: Attackers already exploiting the critical flaw, and Cisco warns they may be able to cover their tracks once they're in
fullText:
Attackers already exploiting the critical flaw, and Cisco warns they may be able to cover their tracks once they're in

Criminals are exploiting a critical Cisco Secure Email Gateway flaw that can turn a malicious email into root access.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-76461, carries a 9.8 CVSS score and affects physical and virtual Secure Email Gateway appliances regardless of their configuration. Cisco says there are no workarounds, so patching is the only fix.

The bug lies in how Cisco's AsyncOS software handles incoming email. An attacker doesn't need to log in: they can send a booby-trapped message through a vulnerable gateway and, if the exploit works, run commands as root.

Which is not exactly what you want from the box tasked with keeping nasty emails out.

Cisco's Product Security Incident Response Team said it became aware of active exploitation in September, although the networking giant hasn't said who is behind the attacks, how long they have been going on, or how many organizations have been compromised. Cisco uncovered the bug while resolving a Technical Assistance Center support case.

Signs suggest at least some Cisco cloud customers were caught up in the attacks. Cisco said it investigated devices belonging to its Secure Email Cloud service and directly contacted customers whose appliances showed indicators of possible compromise. It is now carrying out remediation and recovery work and says all of its Secure Email Cloud devices have been upgraded to AsyncOS 16.5.0-780.

Admins running their own appliances have a little more work to do. Cisco recommends checking logs for signs of suspicious activity, but warns that finding nothing doesn't necessarily mean the system is clean.

Once attackers have root access, Cisco says they could tamper with the logs and cover their tracks. Admins are also being told to check network and firewall logs for anything unusual, rather than relying on the gateway itself for answers.

For virtual appliances suspected of being compromised, Cisco's recovery advice is fairly drastic: preserve the forensic evidence, deploy a fresh VM running fixed software, rebuild the configuration, and rotate credentials and cryptographic material.

Cisco has fixed the bug in AsyncOS releases 15.5.5-014, 16.0.4-302 and 16.5.0-780, with customers strongly encouraged to move to the latter.

There's still a decent-sized target pool out there. The Shadowserver Foundation was tracking more than 400 Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances exposed to the internet as of Monday

The flaw has also landed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, with US federal civilian agencies ordered to remediate it by September 17.

CVE-2026-76461 comes less than a year after attackers exploited another critical AsyncOS flaw, CVE-2025-20393, to break into Cisco Secure Email Gateway appliances and install persistence mechanisms. That bug eventually scored a perfect 10.

For anyone still running an affected gateway, the message is fairly simple: the box designed to inspect hostile email can itself be pwned by one; attackers are already doing it, and there is no workaround to hide behind.  ®

AWS says it can't restore service to Bahrain facilities 6mo after Iran strikes
description: In March, two Amazon data centers in the UAE were struck by drones, while a site was also damaged by a nearby drone hit.
fullText:
Amazon Web Services said Tuesday it can't restore access to cloud-computing facilities in Bahrain and parts of the United Arab Emirates, more than six months after the sites were damaged by drone strikes in the early days of the Iran war.

The company said in an update posted to AWS' health dashboard that the damage at multiple Bahrain-based sites exceeded what its services are designed to withstand.

"After a thorough assessment, we have determined that we are unable to restore access to the resources and data hosted exclusively in this region," AWS wrote.

In a separate post, AWS said it's similarly been unable to recover resources and data stored in one of its availability zones in the UAE. It continues to work to restore two other UAE zones that were affected.

The posts mark AWS' first public update on the incidents since April. Amazon said in March that two of its data centers in the UAE had been directly struck by drones, while a facility in Bahrain was also damaged by a nearby strike. The company told customers to move their workloads to other AWS regions, and warned that instability was likely to continue in the Middle East, making operations "unpredictable."

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed responsibility for the strikes and said it targeted the Bahrain facility for Amazon's support of the U.S. military.

The attacks have raised questions about the security of future data center developments in the Gulf region, which has looked to capitalize on the surge in infrastructure demand tied to the artificial intelligence boom. In May 2025, OpenAI, Nvidia, Oracle and Cisco signed up to be core partners on UAE Stargate, a massive campus that was expected to have 5-gigawatt capacity and cover 10 square miles.

The UAE is now considering revising the project to disperse the facilities across the country, and implementing enhanced security measures, including building some sites underground, using blast-resistant concrete and drone and missile interceptors, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Amazon said it remains committed to supporting its customers in Bahrain and the UAE. The company said it expects to provide further updates on the situation in UAE "in the coming months," and will have more to share for users in Bahrain in early 2027.

title: Movies with their own making-of book
description: There are tons of books about filmmaking and filmmakers, but I have a particular appreciation for books written about just one specific movie. These microhistories (a genre I love) go deep on their…
fullText:
There are tons of books about filmmaking and filmmakers, but I have a particular appreciation for books written about just one specific movie. These microhistories (a genre I love) go deep on their film’s influences, development, production, and extended cultural relevance, and through that can tell us a lot about the power of cinema beyond opening weekend.

Because I’m a psycho, I’ve slowly been accumulating a list of all the books I could find that fall into this category. Some are written by people involved with the film’s production, while others are by journalists or critics. I’ve read several of them but far from all, so this list is aspirational as much as informational.

See below for what I’ve gathered thus far, listed alphabetically by film title. I also created a list on Letterboxd and will update both as I discover more. Let me know if I’m missing any!

fullText:
Samsung has backed a Dutch AI chipmaker in a $231 million funding round, amid a boom in investment in alternatives to Nvidia's graphic processing units.

Euclyd CEO Bernardo Kastrup told CNBC exclusively that the company's 200-million-euro Series A drew backing from Somerset Capital Partners, the Scaleup Europe Fund managed by EQT and Innovation Industries, which all co-led the round alongside Samsung.

The startup, founded in 2024, is designing an AI chip system, with different architecture to GPUs, for inference, including the processor and memory architecture.

Nvidia became the world's most valuable company after its GPUs, originally designed for gaming, were repurposed for training and using AI models, known as inference.

The company has developed a near monopoly over the market for the highest-end chips, but some hyperscalers, alongside startups, are looking to develop their own processors for AI workloads.

OpenAI announced in August that its first AI chip, the Jalapeño, had "industry-leading speed and efficiency." Google, AWS and Meta are all also developing their own AI chips.

"AI is becoming a foundation of economic growth, scientific discovery and national competitiveness, but its potential will remain constrained unless we fundamentally change the infrastructure beneath it," said Kastrup.

Euclyd's systems have yet to be proven at scale in commercial deployments.

But the company said its silicon systems for foundational models will reduce the energy needs and costs of AI data center infrastructure, which is seeing a funding boom.

The company is targeting two revenue streams: selling hardware and physical rack systems to enterprise customers who want secure self-hosted AI inference, and selling its intellectual property to companies that want to develop their own chips based on pre-existing tech.

"Samsung can help us in more ways than money," said Kastrup. "They are one of the biggest memory manufacturers in the world. They do a lot of engineering, they know a lot about systems, they know the supply chain, they have a huge network."

Euclyd aims to begin rolling out its physical chip systems in 2028, with thousands of enterprise customers being served by 2030, Kastrup told CNBC.

title: 'MAGA Act' could rip House seats from Dem states ahead of next presidential race
description: The House GOP proposal would count only citizens for apportionment, with a CIS report saying noncitizens gave Democrat states a net 14 seats.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX: A new House GOP proposal targeting the nation's congressional map could kneecap blue states and dramatically change their representation on Capitol Hill.

Rep. Andrew Clyde, R-Ga., is introducing legislation that would only count citizens when deciding how many House representatives each state gets, called the Make Apportionment Great Again (MAGA) Act.

It would be a fundamental change in congressional representation across the country, particularly hitting states where the most noncitizens live. The U.S. census has traditionally sought to count all people living within the country's borders, regardless of citizenship or even lawful status.

Where Trump, Gop Vs Democrats Redistricting Battle Heads Next In Wake Of Key Court Rulings

According to the U.S. census website, immigrants — both citizens and noncitizens — make up a fifth of the population in California, New Jersey, New York and Florida. Illegal immigrants living in sanctuary jurisdictions are also in theory counted by the census.

A 2024 report by the Center for Immigration Studies (CIS) said immigrants, both legal and illegal, resulted in a "net increase" of 14 seats in Democrat-leaning states. Republican states had 10 fewer seats than they otherwise would have, the report said.

More Than A Quarter-million Noncitizens May Be Registered To Vote In 4 Key States, Dhs Alleges

The legislation would not require a new census after 2020, instead forcing states to rely on existing records to reapportion by sometime in 2027.

It would, however, add a new question to the 2030 census, asking people whether they are a U.S. citizen, U.S. national but not a citizen, an alien lawfully residing in the United States, or an alien unlawfully residing in the United States.

Rnc Legal Victory Clears North Carolina Voter Roll Purge Of Noncitizens Through Jury Responses

But Clyde's bill could see a significant legal battle in the courts, even if passed.

The 14th Amendment to the Constitution states that House seats will be apportioned after "counting the whole number of persons in each State," not specifying citizenship status. It could invite challenges from pro-immigrant groups and left-wing organizations that have long been critical of GOP election efforts.

Jackson Accuses Thomas Of Echoing Infamously Racist Court Decision In Birthright Citizenship Clash

Clyde's bill comes after a video clip resurfaced in July that appears to show Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., claiming she needs more immigrants in her district "just for redistricting purposes."

The video, from a 2021 House Foreign Affairs Committee briefing, shows longtime Democrat Clarke suggesting that the local Haitian community in Brooklyn could "absorb a significant number of these migrants."

"When I hear my colleagues talk about, you know, the doors of the inn being closed, no room in the inn, I'm saying, you know, I need more people in my district, just for redistricting purposes and those members could clearly fit here," said Clarke.

Clarke's office did not respond to a request for comment at the time by Fox News Digital.
