title: Kennedy Center votes to close as Trump threatens to spike renovations
description: The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted to immediately close the bulk of the iconic institution for the next two years.
fullText:
WASHINGTON – The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted to immediately close the bulk of the iconic institution as it prepares for renovations pushed by President Donald Trump and his administration.

The Sept. 15 action from the board ‒ composed primarily of members handpicked by Trump ‒ came during a closed-door meeting on Zoom, according to a source with direct knowledge of the vote.

Yet whether the center can remain shuttered will likely be decided by a federal judge. The action tests U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper's order from May blocking a previous board vote in March to close the Kennedy Center. Justice Department attorneys are asking the judge to vacate a preliminary junction he granted that kept the center open.

Trump, meanwhile, said he won't move ahead on the renovations ‒ which he would fund with his money ‒ unless Cooper's decision earlier in the day keeping Trump's name off the center is overturned on appeal.

"The closing will take place immediately, however, the Renovation and Reconstruction, which is a very large and complex job, cannot begin until such time as the D.C. Circuit rules on the Board's approved name," Trump said in a post on Truth Social. "If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place."

More: Judge blocks Kennedy Center's plan to add Trump's name back on building

The board voted Tuesday to close the Kennedy's Center main building while keeping open a newer, significantly smaller theater wing called the REACH. Trump has said the renovations and repairs will take two years.

Trump-aligned Kennedy Center officials argue that the center has fallen into severe disrepair, posing safety hazards to concertgoers. Even before the formal action to close, the center had already started to wind down holding major shows in its large performance halls.

Rep. Joyce Beatty, the plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging the closure, said the Kennedy Center has historically conducted "phased renovations" to keep the center open during construction.

"This is how major performing arts centers in the country operate," Beatty said. "But donors, patrons, and artists all fled after the unlawful attempt to rename this sacred memorial after Donald Trump."

Beatty added: "Donald Trump only cares about the Kennedy Center for his vanity. That is wrong and it is a breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee."

More: Are Kennedy Center events still happening as closure threat looms?

When Cooper in May blocked the board's March vote to close the center, the judge said the board lacked enough information to make the decision. Since that decision, the Kennedy Center hired an outside vendor that identified leaks and other problems to justify the temporary closure.

At a court hearing Tuesday, Cooper told the federal government's attorneys that nothing from his May order prevents them from conducting routine maintenance work to address the problems cited in the consultant's report, as long as the center remains operating.

In a 22-page written order Tuesday, Cooper blocked the Trump-aligned Kennedy Center board's plan to inscribe Trump's name below the main sign on the building to honor the president's financial support for the center. The judge ruled that the move violated his May order to remove the president's name from the center after it was renamed the "Trump-Kennedy Center" after Trump's takeover of the institution.

"Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," wrote Cooper, an appointee of President Barack Obama. "The board resolution bucks a federal court order and a statute Congress enacted."

A draft resolution prepared for the board to consider proposed 10 different wordings and phrases to recognize Trump's financial support for the center with an inscription below the center's main exterior sign. The resolution, drafted by Kennedy Center officials, warned that Trump would not lead the "fiscal rescue" of the center from potential bankruptcy unless the honorary inscription for him was added.

At the court hearing, Cooper pressed Justice Department attorneys on whether a trust, like the Kennedy Center, can even file for bankruptcy. The attorneys said they did not have an answer.

"Before throwing around these concepts, I would suggest knowing the answer to these questions," Cooper said.

Reach Joey Garrison on X @joeygarrison.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Kennedy Center votes to close as Trump threatens to spike renovations

title: Iran's regime came for teenage twins. Their fate offers a glimpse of Tehran's widening death campaign
description: Iranian twins Taraneh and Romina Rahimi face execution and decades in prison after joining protests, as Iran's death penalty surge draws global alarm.
fullText:
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were 19, still in high school and living with their mother when masked men came for them in the middle of the night.

According to their U.S.-based cousin, the twin sisters were dragged from their beds with bags placed over their heads about a month after they joined anti-regime protests in Isfahan. Their family was given no explanation and spent months searching courts, hospitals and government offices trying to determine where they had been taken.

Four months later, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, was finally allowed to see them at Dowlatabad Prison. She barely recognized her daughters.

One Glaring Issue Goes Unaddressed In Un Chief's High-stakes Talks With Iran's President

Their cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, told The Guardian that the twins had badly swollen and bruised faces, injuries to their elbows, hands and feet, and significant hair loss that he said resulted from guards pulling them by their hair as they were moved between cells. He said their mother also learned that the sisters had been held in solitary confinement.

Now 20, Taraneh Rahimi faces execution over her alleged role in the January protests, while her twin sister could spend decades in prison, in a case unfolding amid a sharp rise in Iran's use of the death penalty.

Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported that Taraneh was sentenced to death and an additional 11 years in prison, while Romina received a 36-year sentence. The sentences were issued by Branch 1 of the Isfahan Revolutionary Court and remain initial-stage verdicts.

The twins are among 16 defendants prosecuted in what has become known as the "Isfahan Shohada Square" case. HRANA said 10 defendants received death sentences and the 16 defendants collectively received 256 years in prison.

The sisters' family says the abuse was intended to force confessions.

Iran Jails Psychologist Over Trump Plea As Regime Demands He Make Americans 'Look Stupid': Family

Nourmohammadi told The Guardian that Taraneh was threatened that prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless she signed a confession. The outlet reported that Taraneh later told the court that admissions attributed to her had been obtained through torture. Her mother was not permitted to attend the trial, according to the family.

Radio Farda separately reported, citing Nourmohammadi, that the sisters suffered physical and psychological abuse and were forced to confess to accusations they deny. The Hana Human Rights Organization told Fox News Digital they have verified the torture allegations.

Concerns about torture extend beyond the sisters. HRANA reported that another defendant in the same case, Ahmadreza Saeidi, told judges during the hearing that the investigating judge personally used an electric stun gun on his neck and genitals. Defense lawyers also reportedly complained that they had not been given access to substantial portions of the case file or adequate time to examine evidence before trial.

The sentences come as rights organizations document a sharp rise in executions across Iran.

Could Narges Mohammadi Unite Iran's Opposition? Husband Says Imprisoned Nobel Laureate Still Fighting

The Washington-based Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran documented 901 executions during the first seven months of 2026, including 56 people executed on political or national-security charges.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, Iran program senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that the executions should be viewed as part of a broader campaign by Tehran to suppress dissent at home.

"Despite the war in the region, despite the drone war, the missile war, the war over the Strait of Hormuz, the real war is the one that's happening on a day-to-day basis inside the Islamic Republic," Ben Taleblu said. "The Islamic Republic is quite literally cracking skulls, cracking down on civil society, on dissidents, on protesters."

Among those imprisoned in Iran's broader crackdown is Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old psychologist whose case Fox News Digital reported in August.

Seyedabdollahi posted an English-language video on Jan. 4 appealing directly to President Donald Trump to support Iranian protesters, according to his relatives and Fox News Digital's previous reporting. He was arrested 10 days later and ultimately sentenced to seven months in prison and barred from government and public services for five years.

His relatives told Fox News Digital that Iranian authorities later pressured him to record another video insulting Trump and Americans and alleged that he was subjected to solitary confinement and torture.

The Hana Human Rights Organization reported Aug. 9 that Seyedabdollahi had been held in Borujen Prison since July 7 and that authorities opened a second case against him on a charge of "propaganda against the system of the Islamic Republic." Hana also confirmed that he was serving a seven-month sentence and had received a five-year disqualification from public and governmental services.

His relatives confirmed to Fox News Digital that authorities have continued pressuring him to say he was a "foreign agent" paid by the U.S. government. They also said authorities revoked his professional license, adding financial pressure on his family.

Ben Taleblu said Tehran has followed a similar pattern after previous periods of external conflict, turning its attention inward against perceived opponents.

Inside Tehran: Iranians Describe Irgc's Brutal Rule, Poverty — Ask Trump To 'Stay The Course'

"We saw this trend in the aftermath of the 12-day war as well," Ben Taleblu said. "Lose a war abroad, come home and pretend like you're the victor."

"Simply here, the Islamic Republic is continuing the longest war it's ever fought, which is the 47-year war against the Iranian people," he added.

Wednesday marks four years since the Sept. 16, 2022, death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish Iranian woman who was detained three days earlier by Iran's morality police over what authorities described as "improper hijab." Her death sparked nationwide protests that became known internationally as the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement. The U.N. said reports that Amini had been beaten in custody warranted an independent investigation, while Iranian authorities maintained that she died of "natural causes."

'Killing Off The Country': Iran Executes Dozens, Arrests 4,000-Plus In War Crackdown

The 2022 uprising was itself part of a longer cycle of unrest. Nationwide demonstrations beginning in December 2017 rapidly spread across Iran and represented the largest challenge to the government since the 2009 Green Movement. The 2017-18 protests were followed by another major nationwide wave in 2019 and then the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom uprising.

Ben Taleblu argued that whenever another major protest movement emerges, Western governments should be prepared to help Iranians communicate with one another and the outside world, particularly when authorities shut down internet access.

"We know every single time another major protest is happening, the way the regime cracks down is to first turn off the internet," he said. "That means the regime fears what comes of coordination between Iranians and fears what comes of when the Iranians are able to send their message outside to the international community."

"The partners of the Iranian people, America, Israel, the West, these are largely all cyber superpowers," Ben Taleblu said. "We should not let the Iranian people continue to die in the darkness."

title: Hochul accused of ‘hit job’ on behalf of teachers’ unions in act of ‘pure censorship’: labor group
description: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is accused of a free speech "hit job" after signing a law letting Letitia James fine groups contacting union members.
fullText:
New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is being accused of conducting a "hit job" on free speech on behalf of teachers unions after she signed a law giving the state attorney general the power to fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union.

Hochul signed a law last week prohibiting people and organizations from using deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union or union representative. The law, which took immediate effect, allows Democratic Attorney General Letitia James to investigate and sue to stop alleged violations, including those involving out-of-state groups. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per incident.

In response, the Freedom Foundation, a conservative nonprofit that campaigns against public-sector unions, including teachers' unions, says New York's new law is a targeted effort to silence its outreach by making its communications vulnerable to government investigations, lawsuits and fines.

CEO Aaron Withe called the law a "hit job." He said the law "isn't about protecting anyone," adding that it instead "exists because government unions in New York are terrified of an inconvenient fact: when public employees learn they don't have to pay union dues, a lot of them stop. So instead of making their case to their own members, union bosses ran to their friends in the legislature and got them to write a law that makes speech illegal."

Nation's Largest Teachers Union Under Fire As Controversial Agenda Puts Century-old Federal Charter At Risk

A spokesperson for Hochul responded by telling Fox News Digital that "Governor Hochul takes fraud of any kind seriously, which is why she signed the legislation prohibiting the false impersonation of union officials to protect workers from being mislead by deceptive communications."

The spokesperson added that "employee organizations and unions play a crucial role in New York's infrastructure as a whole, and the Governor has always championed legislation that supports, protects and uplifts workers across the state."

Fox News Digital reached out to James' office for comment as well. Fox News Digital also reached out to the New York State United Teachers, United Federation of Teachers and the AFL-CIO for comment.

The law allows James to investigate alleged violations, issue subpoenas and ask a court to block communications deemed deceptive. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per violation, including against organizations outside New York.

The New York State American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (NYS AFL-CIO) praised Hochul's decision to sign the bill, which she signed along with two other pieces of legislation related to labor rights. Mario Cilento, president of NYS AFL-CIO, remarked that the law will be "holding individuals accountable for fraudulently claiming to be union representatives."

He said the slate of bills signed by Hochul "put workers first."

In an X post, Hochul similarly framed the bills as prioritizing workers, writing, "Today marks a new day with even more protections, because I'll never stop fighting for our workers."

"New York State gave birth to the labor movement. Over the last five years, I have continued that legacy by fiercely supporting the men and women of labor," wrote Hochul.

Trump Unloads On Aoc, Mamdani For Laughing During Sacred 9/11 Ceremony At Ground Zero

Meanwhile, the Freedom Foundation has mailed and otherwise contacted New York public employees, including teachers, to inform them of their ability to leave their unions and stop paying dues. Nearly 7,500 New York public employees have used Freedom Foundation materials to cancel their union memberships, including more than 1,400 so far this year, according to the group.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Withe pointed to the 2018 Supreme Court decision in Janus v. AFSCME, which held that public-sector employees, including public school teachers, cannot be forced to pay union fees for collective bargaining or other speech because that speech can involve political issues protected by the First Amendment.

He said that while the New York law "lets Letitia James fine the Freedom Foundation for outreach the state decides 'impersonates' a union … all we're doing is telling public employees what already gives them: the right to leave their union and stop paying dues."

"This is an anti-speech law aimed at one kind of speaker," said Withe.

He asserted that the New York law was "copied" from a similar measure in Oregon, which the Freedom Foundation is already challenging in the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. He said his organization will "make the same case here."

Fox News Digital spoke with Ryan Walters, former superintendent of Oklahoma public schools and CEO of Freedom Foundation's education arm, the Teacher Freedom Alliance. Walters called the New York law an example of "pure censorship and targeting of political opponents by Democrats protecting their union bosses."

Inside Teachers' Union May Day 'Dress Rehearsal' Critics Warn Will 'Groom' Students Into Dem 'Foot Soldiers'

"This is such a canary in the coal mine moment where if New York is allowed to do this - an openly socialist mayor, a governor operating as a tyrant doing the behests of the teachers' unions - it's going to go on across the country, and our schools will not be able to improve in that kind of environment," he said, adding, "Where New York goes with this is going to be where the other blue states follow."

He posited that the New York law "shows you how important that power structure is for the Democrat party."

"They have to control the school system to continue to control the country," he said. "Despite elections, they still control these education systems at large. That's why the teachers' unions are enemy number one of progress in this country and why New York needs to be taken on directly for what they're doing."

title: Indonesian shipwreck survivor saw vessel capsize in minutes then waited 10 hours for rescue
description: Rizky Apriansyah was asleep on the top deck of the Virgo Transport 8, the ferry that capsized in Indonesia's Java Sea, when
fullText:
JAKARTA, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Rizky Apriansyah was asleep on the top deck of the Virgo Transport 8, the ferry that capsized in Indonesia's ‌Java Sea, when friends woke him up at around 1 a.m. on Sunday, urging him ‌to grab a life jacket.

At that point, the ship was already heeling at roughly 30 degrees to the left, Rizky told ​Reuters.

Panicked, he and his four friends rushed out of their room. Rizky, who worked as a waiter onboard, recalled seeing waves as high as 3 to 4 metres hitting the vessel multiple times, sending the ship listing even further.

No alarm was rung, he said, and he feared other passengers might not be aware of ‌the impending tragedy.

The ferry company, Virgo ⁠Karya Shipping, told local media they could not comment on the alarm issue because they needed to check with the crew on board at the time.

"When I went out that door, I immediately fell onto the ship's railing. I held on and hugged my friends, then we were swept away by the waves," Rizky said.

In mere minutes, he ​and his ​friends were adrift at sea, holding on to a ​floating 12-kilogram cooking gas cylinder, about 15 ‌meters from the ship.

They watched as the ferry overturned.

"It only took minutes for the ship to capsize, even less than 10 minutes," Rizky said.

They then floated for about 10 hours before another ship spotted them and saved them.

Six people died in the accident and 129 remain missing as of Tuesday as rescuers battled rough seas and strong wind in their operation to find survivors. Some 234 were aboard.

The ferry ‌was travelling about 510 kilometres from Indonesia's second-biggest city of ​Surabaya in East Java to Banjarmasin in Borneo island, roughly ​a 20-hour trip.

It left the port in ​Surabaya on Saturday afternoon, and was reported missing on Sunday morning. Authorities eventually found ‌it inverted around 80 nautical miles (nearly 150 ​km) from the Banjarmasin port.

Rizky ​said since the ship left Surabaya, it had been rocked by high waves. He had only been working onboard for three months. Now he said he is traumatised and would not ​work at sea again.

"I felt overwhelmed, ‌exhausted, suffocated, and just accepted whatever will happen," he said, with his eyes still red ​and minor wounds visible in parts of his body.

title: Mark Zuckerberg is outsourcing his thinking to AI. It shows in his new ‘personal AI agent’ experiment
description: AI can remove costly workplace bottlenecks, but leaders risk losing the dissent and competing views that make better decisions possible.
fullText:
Mark Zuckerberg has access to some of the most sophisticated artificial intelligence systems on the planet. He is also building a company around the idea that AI can dramatically reduce the need for human work.

A recent Reuters investigation offers a revealing glimpse of where that idea can lead. Meta's Project OT envisioned an "AI-native" company in which AI agents would take over much of the work performed by thousands of employees. Teams could become dramatically smaller. Some layers of management could disappear. Zuckerberg himself has been using what Meta calls a "CEO agent," allowing him to retrieve answers that previously required going through several layers of staff.

The attraction is obvious. Every organization contains friction. Meetings take time. Information gets lost between layers. There's push back.  Decisions move slowly. AI can compress all of this.

Yet some friction serves a different purpose. It comes from people who disagree, see problems differently, remember inconvenient facts or ask questions that others would rather avoid.

That distinction matters enormously as AI moves from helping people perform tasks to helping leaders think.

We call these two forms of friction coordination friction and cognitive friction. Coordination friction comes from the mechanics of collective work: scheduling, documentation, data reconciliation, approvals and communication. AI can reduce much of this friction with obvious benefits.

Cognitive friction comes from the resistance between ideas. Two people may look at the same evidence and reach different conclusions because they have different assumptions, experiences or ways of framing the problem. That friction can be uncomfortable. It also can be generative.

This creates a peculiar danger for people at the top of organizations.

Imagine a CEO who once received information through several layers of people. Each layer introduced interpretation. Each person brought a different mental model. Someone might challenge the premise of a question. Someone else might point out an anomaly. Another might say, "We tried this three years ago, and here is what happened."

An AI agent can make that entire process dramatically faster. It can retrieve the information, synthesize it and present a coherent answer.

And coherence can feel like intelligence.

The danger arises when AI becomes a sophisticated mirror.  Instead of creating distance from an existing worldview, it can make that worldview more articulate, comprehensive and persuasive. The user experiences an apparent external intelligence while interacting with a system that has learned from the user's preferences from their previous questions, prompts, assumptions, and accumulated information.

title: When will summer heat end? Study has bad news.
description: A new study finds that in the United States, rather than occurring only during summer, extreme heat events have become more frequent in the months after, too.
fullText:
Sick of sultry Septembers? This story isn't good news for folks who hate the heat.

Around the world, extreme heat is sneaking out of the summer and spreading both earlier into spring and later into fall, a new study suggests.

"We found that over more than half of global land areas, extreme heat seasons are expanding significantly," Casey (Catherine) Ivanovich, a climate scientist at Columbia University and lead author of the new study, told USA TODAY.

The timing of extreme heat matters: It's harder on the body when it comes before folks have gotten used to the season, or if it comes after people have already had to endure months of it, according to a statement from the Columbia Climate School, which is affiliated with the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies.

"In some places, we have a larger expansion of extreme heat during the spring, before the traditional heat season starts," she said. "In other places, there's a much faster expansion of the heat season into fall."

This makes it harder for communities to prepare for, since cooling centers and heat alerts are often organized around a summer calendar.

The study was published Sept. 10 in the journal AGU Advances, a publication of the American Geophysical Union.

"In much of the U.S., we're seeing a larger expansion of the extreme heat season into the fall than the spring," Ivanovich told USA TODAY in an email. "This can unfortunately increase the overlap of extreme heat with other seasonal hazards, such as the wildfire season in the West and the Atlantic hurricane season in the East."

When multiple hazards such as these happen at once or in rapid succession, "they are much more dangerous and impactful than if these events happened in isolation," she added.

The study found that in eastern China, northern Africa and eastern Europe, extreme heat events became more common more rapidly in the two months following their historical heat seasons. The opposite held in western Europe, southern Africa and northwestern India, where extreme heat came predominantly in the two months before.

According to Ivanovich, "heat waves in the spring can catch us off guard before our bodies have acclimated to the heat and before we're ready to utilize cooling strategies like installing air conditioning."

"In the fall, heat waves can be more dangerous if we've already experienced repeated extreme heat events that leave our bodies stressed."

"While recent papers have explored changing average temperatures and how the start and end of the summer season are changing, our study is the first to our knowledge to explicitly measure the change in the timing of extreme heat," Ivanovich told USA TODAY.

In the study, "we also differentiate between dry and humid heat extremes, as these types of climate hazards have distinct impacts." For example, dry heat is harder on crops and ecosystems; humid heat is more dangerous to people, because it limits the body's ability to cool itself by sweating. Adapting to one is not the same as adapting to the other.

To do the study, scientists compared extreme heat events in the 1980s to those more recently (2015 to 2024).

Their analysis found that extreme heat seasons had expanded significantly across just over half the world's land area for dry heat, and just under half for humid heat. And they had expanded lopsidedly, pushing further into spring in some regions and fall in others, according to the Columbia Climate School.

"We can't confirm what share of the signal is due to climate change using observations alone," said Ivanovich, but "it's certainly the primary component of the story."

Overall, according to the study, rising temperatures associated with climate change are likely helping boost extreme heat into new times of year.

"Future studies will allow us to quantify the role of climate change – as well as factors including land use change and natural climate variability – in driving these changes," she told USA TODAY.

Doyle Rice is a national correspondent for USA TODAY, with a focus on weather and climate.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: When will summer heat end? Study has bad news.

title: US military says it destroyed 2 small Iranian boats trying to steal a sea drone
description: The U.S. military said Tuesday that it opened fire and destroyed two small Iranian boats this week that were trying to steal a drone ship in the waters off Iran, the latest back-and-forth fire in the ...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military said Tuesday that it opened fire and destroyed two small Iranian boats this week that were trying to steal a drone ship in the waters off Iran, the latest back-and-forth fire in the stalemated war.

Capt. Tim Hawkins, U.S. Central Command spokesman, said the Iranian boats "recently attempted to take possession of a U.S. unmanned surface vessel" but failed after the military "forcefully responded."

Iranian state media reported Monday that a pair of fishing boats came under attack in Hormozgan province on Iran's southern coast and that several fishermen were reported missing, citing a provincial official.

It is the latest volley of fire in the more than 6-month-old war as both sides seek control over the Strait of Hormuz, where the U.S. has succeeded in recent weeks in loosening Iran's grip over the critical energy shipping corridor. But the impact of the unpopular conflict has driven up the cost of oil and gasoline prices, posing political problems for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of November's congressional midterm elections.

"Oil will drop like a rock as soon as the Military Conflict with Iran is over, and that will not be long," Trump asserted in a social media post Monday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday called the foreign minister of Oman to discuss the Gulf Arab country's efforts to deescalate tensions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the State Department said.

Global oil markets have been further roiled by increased attacks from Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen against Saudi Arabia's shipping and infrastructure.

The new front in the Middle East conflict has cut off or hindered alternate routes for Saudi Arabia to get its oil to the world, including an attack days ago that damaged its biggest pipeline and advances that strengthened the Houthis' ability to choke off Saudi oil exports out of the Red Sea.

Besides the hit to the global economy, new reports out of Washington have detailed the U.S. costs for the war against Iran, the reduction to stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors, and the damage that has been inflicted on American aircraft, bases and diplomatic outposts.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday that the war has cost the Pentagon more than $38 billion through Aug. 1 and will cost up to $3 billion a month or more depending on the intensity of the conflict. That figure largely aligns with what Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has told Congress that the fighting has cost so far.

The CBO said the war is expected to contribute to inflation into the first quarter of next year.

Iranian strikes also have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in the Middle East as well as dozens of American aircraft and drones, according to a report from the Pentagon inspector general released Monday.

Hawkins said Tuesday the sea drone involved in the latest clash is a "Saildrone" — a small, roughly 25-foot (8-meter) craft — which can operate by itself. U.S. Central Command has been using them in the region for several years to surveil maritime traffic.

Hawkins said all of the command's surface drones "remain fully accounted for." The military has long asserted that the technology on the Saildrones is commercially available and not sensitive in nature.

The latest incident, which was reported earlier by Axios, comes a week after Iranian state television reported that the country's navy captured one of the U.S. military's underwater drones at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.

Hawkins said then that an Anduril Dive-LD drone had malfunctioned while it was surveying the waters in the region and the U.S. military no longer had possession of it. He stressed that the drone was defective and noted that it was also an "older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment."

title: Maryland dad blamed 'Satan' after 2-month-old daughter died from horrific head trauma
description: A Maryland father blamed "Satan" for his 2-month-old daughter's fatal head trauma that led to her death, as he and the child's mother are facing child abuse charges.
fullText:
A Maryland couple was arrested after the death of their 2-month-old daughter who suffered head injuries, with the father allegedly telling police the girl's injuries were caused by "Satan slamming a door on the child," according to charging documents and prosecutors.

Oscar Pineda and Katerin Monzon-Alvarado, both 21, are facing charges for first- and second-degree child abuse, first- and second-degree assault and reckless endangerment that carry a maximum possible sentence of 55 years in prison in connection with the death of 2-month-old Aida Mikea Monzon Alvarado, Baltimore Police said, adding that they could face additional homicide charges pending the outcome of the autopsy report.

The baby was taken to Harbor Hospital on Wednesday with what doctors described as "suspicious" severe bruising around her eyes and jawline. A later examination revealed what charging documents describe as "significant head and brain trauma" and "multiple skull fractures" that were not noticed during the initial examination, charging documents state, according to CBS Baltimore.

Idaho Mom Who Claimed Vaccines Killed Her Twin Babies Charged With Murdering Her Kids

The girl's father allegedly claimed to police that his daughter was injured "due to a supernatural force or Satan slamming a door on the child." The mother said her 2-year-old son often jumps on the bed, which caused the baby to fall onto the floor, a prosecutor said at a court hearing on Friday, according to the outlet.

The prosecutor argued that the extent of the girl's injuries could not have been caused by a single fall from the bed.

Police said the girl's mother brought the baby to the hospital on Wednesday after she became unresponsive. The woman initially told police the baby became unresponsive while lying face down in their bed after she was fed.

Alabama Mom Charged With Murder After Toddler Bound, Left To Suffocate For 12 Hours: Cops

Prosecutors said the mother told investigators the child was "freezing and in shock" when she took her to the hospital.

Doctors said the baby "suffered from significant head and brain trauma" and "sustained frontal lobe hemorrhaging and a subdural hemorrhage," according to the charging documents.

Hospital staff could not revive the child, and she died in the hospital.

Both parents later admitted to investigators that they noticed the girl's bruises on Sept. 6 and that she began vomiting the following day. They said they did not seek medical treatment until she was unresponsive on Wednesday.

The pair is Guatemalan nationals, and prosecutors argued they pose "an extreme flight risk."

Both parents were held without bail.

title: AP's refusal to give Trump rights to Butler photo helped fuel Oval Office ban, report claims
description: Trump's administration targeted the Associated Press over photo rights to Evan Vucci's iconic Butler, Pennsylvania, assassination attempt image, according to a NYT report.
fullText:
President Donald Trump's administration targeted the Associated Press (AP) over rights to the iconic photo of the president in Butler, Pennsylvania, taken after an assassination attempt, according to a New York Times report.

The AP has repeatedly sparred with the Trump White House after the president was elected in 2024.

The outlet was banned from the Oval Office and Air Force One shortly after Trump was inaugurated because the AP continued to use "Gulf of Mexico" after the president renamed it the Gulf of America in 2025. The ban has led to a First Amendment battle in court.

However, according to the Times, White House aides also connected the ban to the AP's refusal to give them rights to the infamous photo of the president after he was shot. The Times cited two people briefed on a private lunch with Trump and network anchors in 2025.

Inside Ap's First Amendment Battle With Trump's White House As 'Gulf Of America' Dispute Heads Back To Court

"We're focused on continuing to stand for the right of the public and the press to speak freely without government retaliation or control," a spokesman for the AP told Fox News Digital in a statement in response to the claim.

A source added the White House has not communicated this reasoning to the AP.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Trump was rushed offstage by Secret Service agents after gunfire grazed his upper right ear during his July 13, 2024, rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The attack came months before Trump's re-election and preceded a series of later alleged attempts and reported threats against his life.

The president was mid-sentence, pointing to a chart on illegal immigration under the Biden administration, when gunshots pierced the air at his Butler rally. Authorities identified the gunman as Thomas Matthew Crooks, who fired from the roof of a nearby building.

Two Men Shot At Trump's Butler Rally Sue Federal Government Over Secret Service 'Preventable Failures'

Secret Service agents tackled Trump to the ground. Moments later, as they rose to escort him to his motorcade, Trump emerged from the huddle. Trump raised his fist high in the air, and said "fight" three times, prompting the audience to erupt and chant "U-S-A!" as he exited.

The gunman killed firefighter Corey Comperatore, who was shielding his family, and wounded two other men. A Secret Service sniper killed Crooks during the attack.

A photo of Trump, captured by Evan Vucci of the AP, with his fist raised and blood visible on his face, quickly went viral and landed on the front pages of newspapers across the world.

"I was literally just thinking about doing the best possible job I could, because I knew that this was a moment in American history that I had to be at the top of my game for," Vucci told Fox News Digital in July 2024, after the assassination attempt.

Trump Signs Proclamation Declaring February 9 'Gulf Of America Day' Ahead Of Super Bowl: 'Another Big Win'

"I knew immediately it was gunfire. I trained my lens on the stage, and I saw Secret Service agents going to run to the president, covering him up. And from that moment, I ran to the stage and I got my wide angle lens, and I started making photographs. I went into work mode," Vucci said. "I knew immediately that it was going to be one of the most important things I'll ever photograph, and that I needed to do the best job possible."

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

Vucci switched to a wide angle to ensure the flag flying above got in his shot. He noticed an SUV parked at the side of the stage as Secret Service agents covered Trump and chaos erupted around him. Vucci said he "sprinted" to the side of the stage, assuming it was where Trump would exit, and got in position to snap photos as Trump pumped his fist toward the crowd.

"That's where I was when he was coming down… and that's the photo a lot of people are sharing," he said.

Original article

title: Ex-Dem insider exposes what Harris told top donors days before Biden dropped out: 'Insulting'
description: Lindy Li claims Kamala Harris secretly auditioned for wealthy Democratic donors while publicly insisting Joe Biden would stay in the 2024 race.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, believes Kamala Harris was setting herself up to poach Biden's donors just days before he dropped out of the race — while still telling voters he could win.

Li said she threaded that political needle by staying far away from any criticism of Biden.

"It was all charade. She was auditioning for Biden's endorsement, and the way that she did it was by imposing a fake rule on her staff to not talk about her ascending to the nomination," Li said in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Li's chronicling of the months leading up to Biden's suspended campaign, which are included in her book, "Unburdened," adds more detail about how even those closest to Biden understood that his campaign would likely come to a grinding halt following his disastrous 2024 debate — and even before it.

Ex-biden Staffer Blames Biden's 'Hubris' For The 'Hellscape That We Live In': Report

As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris and someone who had achieved a high profile with the Democratic National Committee (DNC), Li worked with both teams to raise campaign contributions.

In the wake of the election, Li has gone public with much of her insider knowledge, raising the alarm over just how many figures inside the Democratic Party had seen the writing on the wall but remained silent. She also detailed how others, like Harris, quickly moved to prepare themselves for what would happen next.

In Li's view, Harris prioritized face time with donors she knew could soon back her own bid.

"I was on the call; she would host calls with donors and pretend to support Biden and say there's no daylight between Biden and herself. All the while she was auditioning for those very donors," Li said.

Harris Reaches Out To Socialist Mayor Mamdani In Latest Sign She's Shoring Up Support For Possible 2028 Bid

Li recalled how, in one case, Harris addressed donors about Biden's viability as a candidate two days before Biden bowed out.

"It was either on July 19th or July 20th. Actually, I think it was July 19, 2024; Kamala Harris held a call saying that there was no way that Biden would drop out and that she would stick with him until the end. And these were some of the biggest donors in the party," Li recalled.

Biden announced that he would no longer pursue reelection on July 21.

After Biden's announcement, Li recalled that Harris moved aggressively within the Democratic camp to shore up support, insinuating that she had some form of Biden's backing.

"She was flattering people left and right. The first 24 hours were a very intensive charm offensive on her part. And that's how she was able to consolidate it so quickly. She flattered people up the wazoo. It made it abundantly clear that Biden had endorsed her. And Biden initially — I don't know if people know this, but he didn't want to endorse her right away. It took him a while."

Despite the vice president's efforts to maintain her support of Biden and back his viability, Li recalled that some of those same donors didn't buy her story.

Liberal Cnn Anchor Lashes Out At Democrats' Deceit After Jill Biden's Admission About Joe's Debate Showing

"A lot of us have group chats. And the immediate reaction is what an effing waste of time. What a charade, how fake. Like these are like the wealthiest people in the country saying that. They were very aware they were being lied to, that Biden was clearly not okay and to be told that he was okay when he was clearly incapacitated," Li said.

Representatives for Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

title: US drinks giant completes purchase of viral Au Vodka brand for £300m
description: International spirits brand Sazerac has completed its purchase of Au Vodka for a reported £300m
fullText:
US drinks giant Sazerac said it has "big plans" for Au Vodka after completing a takeover reported to value the Welsh business at about £300m.

The Swansea-based vodka brand, known for its gold packaging and viral social media campaigns, was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn in 2015.

With investment from DJ Charlie Sloth it enjoyed rapid growth before being formally acquired by one of the world's largest spirits companies.

Financial terms have not been disclosed, but the Reuters news agency reported the deal values Au Vodka at about £300m ($405m).

Sazerac chief executive Jake Wenz said Au had enjoyed a "phenomenal growth trajectory" since it was founded in Swansea.

"Au Vodka is a brand we've long admired," he said.

"What Charlie, Jackson, and Charlie have achieved in just over a decade is spectacular and rare, and we have big plans for Au as we welcome the brand into the Sazerac family."

Viral vodka brand Au set to sell for £500m to BuzzBallz owner

It's the cocktail taking young drinkers by storm - but the packaging is 'unrecyclable'

He said that the deal would strengthen Sazerac's position in the UK while creating "a path for continued global growth" for the vodka maker.

Au Vodka was founded by friends Charlie Morgan and Jackson Quinn, with broadcaster and DJ Charlie Sloth later joining as an investor.

Known for its distinctive bottles and cans, the company built a large following through social media marketing and celebrity collaborations.

It has grown into one of the UK's best-known premium vodka brands, and employs more than 80 people in south Wales.

Morgan said the founders had started the business with "nothing but an idea and a belief that vodka didn't have to be boring".

"We are proud to have built it into one of the most disruptive brands of this generation," he said.

"With Sazerac, Au can be offered to more people, in more markets, faster than we ever could alone."

The acquisition adds Au Vodka to a portfolio of more than 500 brands owned by Sazerac, including BuzzBallz and Southern Comfort.

title: US strips millions in military aid from Europe and Mideast to back Trump-aligned nations in Americas
description: The Trump administration is stripping tens of millions of dollars in U.S. military assistance from countries in Europe and the Middle East to support conservative-leaning governments in Central and So...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is stripping tens of millions of dollars in U.S. military assistance from countries in Europe and the Middle East to support conservative-leaning governments in Central and South America.

The State Department on Tuesday notified Congress that it will reprogram $52 million in foreign military financing from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru last week and pledged to them additional support as the Trump administration has prioritized the Western Hemisphere in its foreign policy with an emphasis on combating drug trafficking and illegal immigration.

It is just the latest in a series of moves that have reduced either money or troop deployments to Europe in response to President Donald Trump's complaints about NATO allies not spending enough on their defense budgets and other matters. Both North Macedonia and Slovakia are NATO members.

But it also comes as the administration has put particular attention on the Western Hemisphere, aligning deeply with right-wing governments as Trump celebrates a renewal of the 19th century Monroe Doctrine establishing Washington's dominance in the Americas.

Foreign military financing provides recipient countries with U.S. taxpayer dollars to allow them to purchase military equipment from American defense contractors.

The State Department said the funds would be used to "combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal," adding that the Western Hemisphere has been historically neglected in U.S. military assistance.

"These funds will prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere," the department said in a veiled jab at China, which has increasingly sought to boost its presence in Latin America.

The shift of money does not eliminate foreign military financing for Tunisia, Iraq, North Macedonia or Slovakia, although the exact amount remaining for those countries was not immediately clear.

The State Department said, though, that the current distribution of financing does "not align with the administration's prioritization of" the Western Hemisphere.

title: Teenage soldier 'let down' after sexual assault
description: A court martial hears that two senior officers did not deal properly with allegations made by the soldier.
fullText:
A teenage soldier was "let down" by two senior officers when she "told each of them enough to understand that she may have been sexually assaulted" five months before she took her own life, a court martial has heard.

Royal Artillery Gunner Jaysley Beck, from Cumbria, was found dead in her barracks at Larkhill Camp in Wiltshire on 15 December 2021, months after former Battery Sgt Michael Webber "pinned her down" and sexually assaulted her.

Although the 19-year-old reported the incident, the chain of command failed to properly deal with the case, the court was told.

Maj James Hook and Col Samantha Shepherd are on trial accused of conduct prejudicial to good order and service discipline.

The Service Prosecution Authority charged Hook and Shepherd over their handling of the case earlier this year.

Injured horse rider backs road safety campaign

Mayor launches hunt for lost piece of gold chain

Sex abuse PE teacher on remand ahead of sentencing

Commander Patterson, prosecuting, said Hook - who was a captain at the time - did not treat the report from Gunner Beck "in a manner consistent with its seriousness".

He also told the court that Shepherd "deliberately misreported what she had been told".

At the first day of the trial at the Military Court Centre in Catterick, North Yorkshire, the court heard that Webber sexually assaulted Gunner Beck during a team training away day at Thorney Island, near Emsworth in Hampshire, on 12 July 2021.

The team event extended into the early hours of 13 July, until Gunner Beck and Webber were left drinking alone together when he "pinned her down", touched her leg and tried to kiss her multiple times.

The former Warrant Officer was jailed for six months last year after he admitted the offence against Gunner Beck.

Following the sexual assault, Gunner Beck phoned a colleague and confided in them before she spent the night asleep in her car out of fear that Webber would assault her again.

Lance Bombardier Drew Tudor - who had been drinking with Gunner Beck and Webber earlier that night - found her in a "distressed" and "visibly shaken" state in her car the following day.

He added that he "pleaded" with Gunner Beck to pass the report up the chain of command.

Tudor said he was not in a position to ask Gunner Beck the "specific details" but he would have "assisted her" if she had divulged full details about what had happened with Webber.

"What she said was he tried it on with her, he touched her or tried to touch her," he told the court.

Tudor later found Hook and brought him to the car so that Gunner Beck could tell him about the sexual assault too.

Hook agreed that the incident was "serious" and later phoned a more senior officer at the barracks to report that Webber had "made a pass" at Gunner Beck.

He also gave her until noon to decide if she wanted to file a complaint against Webber.

Patterson said Shepherd discussed the incident with Gunner Beck on a walk but then deliberately failed to pass all the information on to Capt Mae King - the adjutant at the 14 Regiment Royal Artillery, who was responsible for discipline.

He said Shepherd failed to mention the touching or attempted touching and said there was "no contact", despite being questioned by King.

In a prepared statement given to military police, Shepherd said she believed she had disclosed the touching allegation but she said she could not be sure.

Patterson said the prosecution's case was that it was "simply not possible, equally not credible, that Capt King had forgotten about being told about the touch" and that Shepherd "deliberately decided to suppress detail about touching" to prevent the service police getting involved with the case.

"It is not Col Shepherd's job to edit information - she should have told the truth," he told the court.

"She knew this would go to the service police."

King told the court that Shepherd had said that Webber had made an "inappropriate pass" at Gunner Beck.

"I confirmed that he hadn't kissed her, that he hadn't touched her and it had been an attempt as opposed to an act," she said.

King made a range of consultations - including with the Royal Military Police (RMP) - before she made the recommendation to Shepherd about a course of action based on what she had been told.

She added that the RMP ruled the incident was "not a crime" because "there was no touching".

The Army apologised after an inquest into Gunner Beck's death found that the handling of her complaint against Webber had played "more than a minimal contributory part into her death".
