title: In Puerto Rico, even when it doesn’t rain, it pours
description: The scramble to find water is a daily survival routine for residents in Puerto Rico due to widespread service interruptions and extreme drought.
fullText:
Milagros Pica Quiñones' small concrete home is an untamed menagerie of bottles, paint buckets, bleach and laundry detergent jugs.

The 96-year-old grandmother in the impoverished oceanfront town of Loiza, in Puerto Rico's northeast, sees "the thinnest thread of water" trickling from her faucet most days before service is shut off from 10 p.m. until dawn.

"I drag the buckets away with whatever strength I have and I cover them," Pica Quiñones said. "Three buckets in the bathroom. One in my kitchen. Outside, I have three, two-gallon buckets. In front of the house: 15 smaller, gallon-sized containers. Next to a wall – 10 large bottles."

The scramble to find water – collecting it in small vessels and cisterns – is a daily survival routine for hundreds of thousands of other US citizens on the island due to widespread service interruptions. The most vulnerable – the elderly, the sick, low-income people – are forced to bear the heaviest burden.

Billed as a beautiful and vibrant tourist destination, Puerto Rico is home to 3.2 million Americans who face an exhausting daily struggle for necessities like clean, running water. Pica Quiñones, whose showers consist of dipping a red Solo cup into a bucket, thinks about water all the time.

The US territory's fragile water situation reached a new critical point over the summer – exacerbated by drought and what experts say is mismanagement and aging infrastructure, including a lack of investment and maintenance. On Friday, people living in the capital of San Juan and nearby communities completed their third full week on mandatory water rationing schedules.

Forced to endure up to two days without running water, residents must rely on bucket baths and dry shampoo, use bottled water for cooking and making coffee, paper plates and plastic utensils to eat, and occasionally forgo laundry, housecleaning and toilet flushing. All while their water bills keep coming.

"When you have a drought colliding with an aging infrastructure, that's more than a drought. That's a humanitarian crisis, and it's a crisis which is deep," said Northeastern University chemistry professor Eugene Smotkin, who lives in Old San Juan with his wife. "It's not a drought story."

Puerto Rico Gov. Jenniffer González-Colón declared a state of emergency July 31 due to the drought. It's unknown how long the rationing measures will remain in place, she said.

"This is a situation that we never expected to happen," the Republican governor told CNN earlier this month, referring to the drought.

The US Department of Agriculture approved a drought disaster declaration on the island, allowing farmers and agricultural producers in 26 municipalities to access emergency loans, the governor's office announced Wednesday.

The governor told MS NOW this week she was "not ruling out" asking Washington for a national emergency declaration, which would unleash massive federal funding for Puerto Rico. Her government, González-Colón said, need to "exhaust all the local assets, all the resources before asking for a national declaration of emergency."

"I totally understand the frustration," she said of island residents who blame the government for the longtime water woes, acknowledging a lack of maintenance to the island's infrastructure.

The capital of San Juan recorded its driest month on record in more than 120 years in July, said Emanuel Rodriguez, a hydrologist at National Weather Service in San Juan.

Most of the island archipelago is experiencing moderate to extreme drought conditions, affecting more than 3 million people, according to the US Drought Monitor.

Lakes and streams – some at or near record lows – are losing water amid a rainfall deficit that could last months, Rodriguez said.

"We could stay below normal (rainfall levels) at least until January," he added.

The water emergency is also a consequence of the deteriorating infrastructure, particularly a series of recent ruptures in the so-called Superaqueduct, a crucial 72-inch pipeline that carries potable water 50 miles along the northern coast to the densely populated San Juan metro area.

Since the pipeline's rupture in June, the Puerto Rico National Guard and government agencies from throughout the island have been distributing potable water from cistern trucks, according to the governor's office.

The governor's office and the Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Carlos Pesquera, a civil engineer and former secretary of transportation and head of public works who was appointed by the governor as an adviser on the water crisis, said the drought "is the immediate trigger" of the current emergency, "but it does not fully explain the vulnerability" of the water system.

"Puerto Rico has aging infrastructure, significant water losses and areas where greater redundancy and resilience are needed," Pesquera, a member of the pro-statehood governing party, told CNN via email.

Before the recent ruptures, nearly 60% of water treated by the aqueduct and sewer authority was lost mostly due to "inaccurate meters, unauthorized water consumption, or water main leaks," according to a 2019 report on the island's infrastructure by the American Society of Civil Engineers.

Hilda Rodríguez, the 58-year-old executive director of a San Juan nonprofit, has been keeping a log of waterless days at her home in the Monteflores neighborhood in the Santurce section of the capital. She started it five years ago, using a water droplet emoji 💧 to track on her cell phone the days without water.

This year, the log shows more than 200 days without water.

In 2025, there were 175 days. The previous year: 142 days. In 2023, 100 days. And 136 days in 2022. A year earlier, 22 days.

"I needed to write all this down because no one would believe me," she said with a laugh. "In Puerto Rico, we make a joke of everything. It's the best way to survive all the things that happen to us – one way to escape as we keep going."

"It's one stumble after another," said Rodríguez, who has also been tracking every phone complaint she's made to the water utility over the years. "Just when you think you're finally getting back up, something else happens."

In another Santurce neighborhood, Anna Andresian and a group of other residents have been keeping an online log of water and power outages since 2024, when 57 days were affected by water outages and 58 days were affected by power outages. So far this year, the log shows, residents have spent more than 140 days with no water and 27 days without electricity.

Puerto Ricans, including the more than 2 million living in the San Juan metro area, have long endured major droughts made worse by the aging water system.

Severe droughts caused water restrictions, affecting more than a million people, from 2014-2016, and more recently in 2020.

"The water problem in the San Juan area has been with us for years," Rodriguez said. "Every year it gets worse. It's draining, a constant state of worry. It is no way to live."

During a 1994 drought, rationing left the San Juan metro area with water available only every second or third day, according to a 2020 report commissioned by the American Society of Civil Engineers. On days when water was available, the pressure in some communities would arrive after midnight and fade by dawn, the report said.

In 1995, with water service only two or three days a week, Rodriguez purchased and paid to install a 600-gallon cistern for about $1,000. If she were to do it now, she said it would cost her more than twice as much.

At the time, the island's water utility responded to the 1994 drought by vowing to end shortages with the $1 billion construction of the Superaqueduct and its interconnections, as well as dredging the main source of water for the San Juan area, the Carraízo reservoir.

With a capacity of 75 million gallons of water per day, the Superaqueduct went into service in 2000.

After more than a quarter century of service, the Superaqueduct's recent breaks exposed a key weakness in Puerto Rico's water system: The heavy reliance on a single, long-distance transmission line without an equivalent backup during a major interruption requires sustained attention and investment, according to Pesquera.

He was appointed as a special adviser for water infrastructure after last year's rupture and prepared a report for the government on improvements to alleviate the island's water problems.

"The Superaqueduct was originally designed as a complimentary water source. Its purpose was to reinforce existing systems and make the metropolitan (San Juan) network stronger, not to replace traditional water sources," he wrote in his report.

González-Colón has said at least $7 billion in federal funds had been committed to water infrastructure improvement projects. The lack of maintenance and investment in the water system dates back decades, she said earlier this week, and the destruction of hurricanes Irma and Maria made matters worse.

For Smotkin, the water crisis reflects the island's history of structural neglect and systemic abandonment by both local and federal authorities. The water woes must be seen in the context of Puerto Rico's dependency on the United States.

"The enduring image is of people standing with bottles and jugs, spending their lives trying to obtain something as elementary as water because the infrastructure that should have delivered it had failed them," said Smotkin, who has lived on the island nearly 25 years and works to bring renewable energy sources to Puerto Rico.

On a recent Wednesday afternoon, Lourdes Tañon, a resident of Trujillo Alto, a municipality southeast of San Juan, was on her way to check the cistern at the home of her mother. Suddenly, it started to rain.

The driver of another car stopped, putting his hands out the window as if to capture the falling droplets, she recalled.

"Getting wet under the first rain of May is a custom here because it supposedly brings good luck," she said. "People go outside and get wet. That's what it feels like now when it rains. We're all praying for more rain."

In 2017, Hurricane Maria struck nine days before the grand opening of Hector Rosa's restaurant, Rosa Cocina Libre, in San Juan's Cupey district. The opening was delayed for five months.

Now he finds himself confronting another crisis, one he believes could have been prevented. His mornings begin by turning on the faucets to see if water is running.

If there is no water, Rosa scrambles to figure out where to get it and how quickly. The restaurant has a cistern and two additional mobile tanks, with a combined capacity of about 2,000 gallons. He must fill up the three tanks at least once a day to keep the restaurant running. He often questions how much longer he can keep operating in Puerto Rico, Rosa said.

"I love my island and I love to be here in Puerto Rico," he said. "I want to be part of the island but it's like having your hands tied every single year — every single month it's something."

The water crisis has become impossible to ignore anywhere Eduardo Caldazo goes.

At his apartment in Isla Verde, one of the island's busiest tourist areas, and at his restaurant-bar, Calle Sin Salida in San Juan, there is no warning about when the water will vanish or return.

He relies on a 400-gallon water tank to keep his restaurant operating four days a week but keeping it filled is a full-time job.

"This is now our daily life," he said. "I know it won't be fixed."

Rafael Cabrera, a 64-year-old university professor, lives in a 30-apartment condominium complex in Monteflores, just south of Machuchal. In 2022, residents raised nearly $100,000 to purchase a pump and cistern to remedy intermittent water service problems. The cistern, which holds nearly 4,000 gallons, went unused until last year, when residents were issued the required water utility permits to activate it, Cabrera said.

"The hardest part is lacking hope about a problem that seems to have no solution," he said.

Some residents said hope is elusive given the island's litany of miseries – from natural disasters to a bankrupt government to a financial control board that manages funding for infrastructure.

"The frustration is understandable, but it is also important to recognize how complex it is to restore a water distribution system after an extended interruption," Pesquera told CNN when asked about residents' criticism. "Residents and businesses need the most realistic information possible about when service will actually reach their area."

In Loiza, Pica Quiñones' great-granddaughter, Modesta Irizarry, drives around helping elderly neighbors. She collects water from cistern trucks, distributes donated packs of bottled water and food, and leads water truck drivers to the homes of the bedridden. Almost every day, she makes time to check on her great-grandmother.

"I find many older adults alone in subhuman conditions with no one to care for them," she lamented, her voice fading.

Irizarry has helped her community in the aftermath of hurricanes, during the Covid-19 pandemic, and other emergencies. The despair over the water crisis, she said, is similar to life after Hurricane Maria.

"I wish I had more hands. There are people who, no matter how much they need it, won't ask for help. They won't let you in because of shame. The suffering is so great."

Her great-grandmother, meanwhile, spends part of her days filling up her menagerie of bottles and containers.

"Whenever we have water, I fill every bottle and bucket I can find. I've never had to live like this – not even after the worst storms," Pica Quiñones said.

title: Japan says its surveillance drone probably crashed off its northwestern coast
description: Japan's air force said one of its long-distance surveillance drones is believed to have crashed into the sea during a flight Tuesday off the country's northwestern coast.  There were no immediate deta...
fullText:
TOKYO (AP) — Japan's air force said one of its long-distance surveillance drones is believed to have crashed into the sea during a flight Tuesday off the country's northwestern coast.

There were no immediate details on the nature of the mission of the uncrewed RQ-4B aircraft, also known as Global Hawk. So far, there was no indication of foul play, but officials said the cause of the presumed crash was under investigation.

The Air Self-Defense Force said the drone had trouble connecting with a communication device about one and a half hours after taking off from the Misawa Air Base. Three minutes later, it disappeared from the radar and was last seen 50 kilometers (31 miles) off the coast of Tottori, the ASDF said.

Later Tuesday, a fighter jet and a Japan Coast Guard patrol ship spotted debris believed to be from the Global Hawk. After examining photos of the debris, the ASDF said the drone is believed to have crashed just after disappearing from the radar.

The cause of the Global Hawk's presumed crash is still under investigation, the ASDF said. There have been no reports of injury or damage related to the crash.

The drone is one of three Global Hawks owned by the air force and deployed at its Misawa Air Base in the northern prefecture of Aomori. Losing one could be a setback for Japan's surveillance capability.

The drones are considered valuable because they can conduct long-range missions and are able to fly at a height of about 60,000 feet (18.3 kilometers) and can fly continuously for up to 36 hours. They allow Japan to easily monitor areas on the Asian mainland, including North Korea and China.

Japan is trying to adapt to changing times and develop defense strategies that use drones, including those for combat, artificial intelligence and new methods of warfare. Under its five-year plan established in 2022, the country has doubled its defense spending to about 2% of its gross domestic product to build up its Self-Defense Forces' offensive role to counter China's growing assertiveness.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government is now preparing new security and defense strategies, expected to be unveiled later this year.

Beijing has criticized Japan's defense buildup as "new militarism."

title: Indian police detain driver who hit female biker in viral video
description: The incident has sparked a broader discussion about the harassment and hostility faced by female motorcyclists.
fullText:
Police in India have detained a man after footage appearing to show a car striking a female motorcyclist in the city of Gurugram near India's capital Delhi sparked national outrage.

The incident took place on Sunday when Shivani Chauhan was riding with a group of motorcyclists.

A video recorded by a camera mounted on her bike appears to show a white car moving close and hitting her motorcycle. Chauhan falls on to the road as her motorcycle skids away, while the car continues moving.

The clip, shared by Chauhan on Instagram, has gone viral, prompting police to open an investigation. The driver, identified as Kalyan Bainsla, has denied hitting her deliberately.

On Tuesday, Gurugram police spokesperson Sandeep Kumar confirmed to the BBC that Bainsla, a gym owner from Palwal in Haryana state, had been detained. Police said he had borrowed the car from another man.

The case was initially registered under sections of the law which deal with rash driving and acts endangering life or personal safety. Police later added "attempted murder" to the charges.

In an interview with Aaj Tak news channel, Bainsla claimed that members of the biking group had repeatedly overtaken his car before slowing down in front of it. He said he lost control near a U-turn while trying to avoid Chauhan's motorcycle.

Bainsla also said he did not initially realise that Chauhan was a woman and maintained that he had asked her and another rider to slow down.

He claimed he drove away because the motorcyclists were shouting abuses and he feared that he and his relatives would be attacked.

"Had I stopped right then, those people would have beaten us up," he told the channel.

Chauhan has disputed his account. In a video posted on Instagram after the crash, she said the car had begun following her group shortly after they started their ride.

She alleged that its occupants became hostile and asked her to stop after she told the driver to keep a safe distance. Chauhan said she continued riding because she feared the car might block her, while a friend riding behind tried to shield her motorcycle.

She also alleged that the men in the car appeared to be intoxicated. The police have not said whether alcohol tests were conducted.

But Bainsla's lawyer, Naveen Bainsla, denied the allegation, telling the ANI news agency that his client had not been drinking and was travelling with relatives. He also rejected the description of the incident as a deliberate "hit-and-run case", arguing that it was a case of negligent driving.

After Bainsla publicly denied hitting her deliberately, Chauhan posted another video on Monday night challenging his version of events.

She said the footage showed which vehicle had been moving towards the other. She also rejected his claim that he had not realised she was a woman.

Chauhan also questioned why Bainsla had not stopped to check on her. "I could have been gravely hurt or broken my bones. I could've died on the spot," she said.

Chauhan sustained minor injuries, according to reports, but her protective gear is believed to have prevented more serious harm.

The footage has prompted widespread anger online and a broader discussion about the harassment and hostility female bikers say they face on Indian roads.

Several women riders shared their experiences of being followed, filmed without consent or challenged to race, particularly when they were riding high-powered motorcycles.

Divya Sandhu, a riding coach who was involved in a similar collision a decade ago, told NDTV channel that attitudes had changed little since then.

"It's very common for people to joke about women's driving skills," she said.

Another motorcyclist, Pallavi Singh, said some women concealed their hair and wore full protective clothing partly to avoid being identified and harassed while riding.

title: Inquiry blasts hospital for failure to protect babies after nurse Lucy Letby convicted of 7 murders
description: An English judge issued a scathing report on Tuesday, blaming dysfunctional management and a “complete failure at all levels” to protect babies at the hospital where neonatal nurse Lucy Letby was conv...
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — An English judge issued a scathing report on Tuesday, blaming dysfunctional management and a "complete failure at all levels" to protect babies at the hospital where neonatal nurse Lucy Letby was convicted of murdering seven newborns.

The inquiry into baby deaths found the Countess of Chester Hospital, in northwestern England, could have saved some infants if staff had acted sooner when children began collapsing, Justice Kathryn Thirlwall said.

"Errors were made by nurses, doctors and managers," Thirlwall said. "There was also complete failure at all levels to invoke safeguarding procedures at any point."

Letby, 36, is serving a life sentence for the murders of seven babies and attempted killing of seven others. She has maintained her innocence, and a defense team backed by dozens of scientists who have questioned the evidence against her are seeking to clear her name.

Thirlwall's inquiry didn't review Letby's convictions, but looked at how institutional failures exposed babies to harm at the hospital, and how staff and management responded and treated parents.

She focused on the failure of staff to intervene when it became clear someone was deliberately harming babies.

"How many lives could have been saved had the hospital acted differently?" she said. "It is clear that some babies would have been saved and some attacks would have been prevented if action was taken earlier."

Letby was convicted in 2023 of the murders of seven infants and attempted murders of six others — including two attempts on one child. A case in which jurors couldn't reach a decision was retried and Letby was convicted of another attempted murder. She was sentenced to 15 life terms with no chance of release — only the fourth woman in the United Kingdom to receive such a term.

Prosecutors said that she harmed babies in ways that left little trace, including injecting air into their bloodstreams, administering air or milk into their stomachs via nasogastric tubes, poisoning them with insulin and interfering with breathing tubes.

She was the only employee on duty in the neonatal unit when the children collapsed or died between June 2015 and June 2016. Prosecutors described her as a "constant malevolent presence."

Thirlwall's report describes how numerous children were harmed, but concerns either weren't raised or suspicions weren't elevated to managers.

"This did not happen," Thirlwall said. "The collapses and deaths continued."

Even once the hospital began to review the spike in infant mortality and connections to Letby's work shifts — and even after the nurse had been placed on administrative duties in July 2016 — police weren't called until May 2017. Letby remained at the hospital until her arrest more than a year later.

Lawyers for Letby tried unsuccessfully to halt the inquiry by saying it could reach the wrong conclusions if her convictions are later reversed.

Defense attorney Mark McDonald said that the conclusions of the inquiry were tainted by errors at trial and accepting that Letby intentionally killed the children.

"The alternative narrative identified by nearly 30 internationally renowned experts has not been properly considered," McDonald said. "The inquiry would have been able to hear an alternative account — one that said that insulin results were unreliable, one that said the deaths did not stop when Lucy left the unit."

Thirlwall said that she didn't consider the debate over Letby's guilt because the Court of Appeal had rejected her legal challenges "with a very clear result." Thirlwall said the people challenging the evidence hadn't been at the trial and she said "all of this noise" caused additional distress to parents "who have already suffered far too much."

McDonald has presented new evidence to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, or CCRC, which looks into possible injustices and could trigger another court challenge.

A review of the medical evidence used at trial by a panel of experts convened by McDonald found no sign of a crime and concluded that natural causes or bad medical care led to the demise of each of the newborns.

The group of international experts in neonatology and pediatrics found there were inadequate staffing levels, and medical workers lacked proper skills, misdiagnosed ailments and acted slowly in treating acutely ill babies.

title: Explainer-From hallucinating AI chatbots to wiping out humanity: How did we get here?
description: The heads of America's leading AI labs came together in a rare show of unity over the weekend to call for a pause in the technology's development, warning that it
fullText:
Sept 16 (Reuters) - The heads of America's leading AI labs came together in a rare show of unity over the weekend to call for a pause in the technology's development, warning that it could soon improve on its own and slip beyond human control.

The remarks, from fierce business rivals Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman and xAI's Elon Musk, show how quickly AI has advanced, from the ‌hallucination-prone ChatGPT of 2022 towards what many see as a critical milestone: recursive self-improvement.

WHAT IS RECURSIVE SELF-IMPROVEMENT?

The holy grail of AI is the idea that an AI system could become capable of improving itself, with little to ‌no help from humans, and allowing each advance to help produce the next one.

This has appealed to researchers as it offers the prospect of rapid breakthroughs in fields ranging from medicine to engineering.

The CEO warnings follow reports of swarms of AI agents - systems designed to pursue goals and take ​actions on a user's behalf - that colluded to breach websites and AI repositories.

Warnings about AI's risks are not new. But they took on added urgency this month after researchers in leading AI labs attached both a timeline and a probability to those concerns.

Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned AI could kill us all by the end of the decade. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's alignment science lead, echoed Coxon's warning, saying there was a more than 10% chance of such an event within the next decade.

Behind these warnings is a growing belief that RSI is finally within reach, with some AI executives putting it three to five years away.

The concern is that AI could become capable of improving itself before researchers have developed reliable methods to align, monitor and control increasingly powerful systems.

In an essay published ‌over the weekend, Amodei warned that recursive self-improvement could eventually outrun humanity's ability to ⁠understand and control AI systems if pursued without sufficient safeguards.

HAS AI SHOWN ANY INDICATION OF HARM?

There have been no major instances of AI intentionally harming humans, but models in development at OpenAI and other labs have in recent months escaped testing environments, broken rules and hacked websites.

In one high-profile case, rogue OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face, seizing control of servers at the open-source platform and trying ⁠to cover their tracks.

Researchers worry that future systems could become increasingly difficult to monitor, particularly as some newer training methods reduce human visibility into how models arrive at conclusions.

title: As the world debates the risks of AI, China closes the technology gap with the US
description: As the rapid development of artificial intelligence triggers a renewed debate about its risks, the United States and China keep racing to develop increasingly powerful models even as they express thei...
fullText:
HONG KONG (AP) — As the rapid development of artificial intelligence triggers a renewed debate about its risks, the United States and China keep racing to develop increasingly powerful models even as they express their own concerns.

The U.S. has outpaced China and other countries for years in AI model capabilities, research, citations and other areas. But China has been rapidly catching up as an AI superpower even as U.S.-led restrictions have blocked China from accessing some of the most advanced technologies, including the cutting-edge chips and the machines to make them.

Experts and recent reports, like one by the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence, said China has emerged as an AI counterweight to the U.S. and this year appears to be erasing the U.S. lead.

"The gap between U.S. and Chinese models is narrow and fragile," said Samm Sacks, a senior fellow at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies' Institute for America, China, and the Future of Global Affairs.

The current debate takes on greater importance ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping's expected visit to Washington this month to meet U.S. President Donald Trump, and as experts say the future of AI will depend significantly on what China and the U.S. do and don't do.

Here's a quick look at some of the most important Chinese AI models and the concerns in both Washington and Beijing:

Beijing-based startup Moonshot AI made a splash with the release of Kimi K3, taking Silicon Valley by surprise with capabilities close to U.S. rivals. It was ranked No. 3 globally in model intelligence in July, shortly after its release, behind Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, according to AI benchmarking platform Artificial Analysis. But Kimi K3 now ranks ninth, behind new frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and SpaceXAI, indicating China's AI lead is fluid.

AI startup darling DeepSeek was the first to upend global stock markets by proving Chinese AI models are capable of challenging the U.S. lead. The company's R1 model, released in January 2025, was more cost-effective than similar U.S. models. In April, DeepSeek previewed its powerful V4 model, saying it has big improvements in knowledge, reasoning and "agentic" capabilities, referring to the ability to plan and execute multiple, complex steps with limited human guidance.

The powerful GLM-5.2 from startup Z.ai that rolled out in June raised Silicon Valley eyebrows with comparisons to the most advanced Anthropic and OpenAI models. Z.ai then launched GLM-5.3 in August with improved coding and agentic capabilities that pushed it up the global AI model rankings.

In July, China's Alibaba previewed its Qwen3.8-Max model, which the tech giant said was its most powerful model in the series, challenging Anthropic's Claude Fable and OpenAI's GPT.

China's state security minister has warned artificial intelligence poses a range of potential threats to the country, from political and ideological security to cyberattacks, data leaks and challenges to governance.

In an article published Sunday, Chen Yixin said the technology could threaten China's political, institutional, and ideological security if used by "hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives."

Some individuals might use AI-generated deepfake audio and video to create "political rumors" on a massive scale, he wrote.

Chen specifically mentioned the capabilities of Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT as examples of how AI could be used to more easily identify and "weaponize" cybersecurity vulnerabilities. He warned certain nations and groups can now "execute complex hacking tasks."

Top Chinese leaders have said China should accelerate the AI development and pursue technological self-reliance. But they also noted the need to control the risks and establish a global framework for AI governance.

The U.S. has accused China's AI developers of engaging in what it has called "industrial-scale distillation," in which AI models are trained to copy or imitate the capabilities of more powerful ones.

In the most comprehensive report by the government to date, the FBI and the National Security Agency and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said Sept. 8 that Chinese AI developers extracted capabilities from some of the most advanced AI models in the U.S. in "aggressive, malicious, and targeted distillation activities."

Also on Sept. 8, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told an event that "the Chinese distill our models and they can never get ahead of us."

China has rejected the claims and said distillation is commonly used across many AI companies. It asked the United States to refrain from making "unfounded accusations" and accused the U.S. of pursuing a "monopoly of the AI industry."

Distillation is a standard technique used across the AI industry, but the U.S. agencies leveled a more specific accusation that Chinese firms used unauthorized access and other methods to extract restricted capabilities from American frontier models, said Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute's Center for China Analysis.

"These are still contested allegations at this point but I think the strategic implication is already important," she said.

The United States spent a lot energy into controlling the inputs into frontier AI, especially chips. But now "it seems that it is finally discovering that it may also have to think about the outputs of frontier AI as a form of technology transfer," Lee said.

"The U.S. labs spend enormous amounts of compute pushing out the frontier. But Chinese developers can learn from those systems," she said. "And Chinese companies then (can) release very capable open-weight models that spread globally."

Castillo reported from Beijing.

title: Saudi Arabia reports wide-ranging security alerts after week of strikes
description: Saudi Arabia issued security alerts over a range of territory on Tuesday, including in the holy city of Mecca and second-largest
fullText:
RIYADH/DUBAI, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia issued security alerts over a range of territory on Tuesday, including in the holy city of Mecca and second-largest city Jeddah, following a week of attacks from Iran-aligned fighters that have drawn it deeper into the Middle East war.

The alerts were swiftly ‌lifted and Saudi authorities did not immediately report whether any incoming projectiles had landed, nor was there any immediate claim of responsibility for attacks.

But the alerts were the ‌widest ranging since an escalation in the conflict last week, and the alarm in Mecca was the first of the war in the city, which houses shrines sacred to all Muslims.

The Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen have announced a number ​of major attacks on Saudi Arabia over the past week, including strikes on an air base on Monday they said were in retaliation for airstrikes on Yemen.

Saudi Arabia has blamed a separate pro-Iranian movement, based in Iraq, for an attack on Friday that knocked out one of the Kingdom's most important oil transport routes, the East-West Pipeline across the Arabian desert.

A Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen said 13 civilians had been wounded in Monday's attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia.

The Iran-backed fighters launched a lightning advance along Yemen's western coast last week, culminating in the seizure ‌of an island in the mouth of the Red Sea.

NEW THEATRE ⁠STRENGTHENS IRAN'S HAND

The escalation in a new theatre in the Middle East conflict has strengthened Iran's hand in its war with the U.S. and further jeopardised global oil supplies.

Officials from a Saudi-backed Yemeni government, which is based in the south of the country and opposes the Houthis, said the ⁠Saudi and Yemeni air forces had been responding to Houthi advances by stepping up aerial bombardment of Houthi targets. That included strikes near the historic Red Sea port of Mocha, which the fighters captured last week.

But the Yemeni officials acknowledged that the Houthis had now taken effective control over almost the entire western coast of the country along the Red Sea.

"The Houthis are being put under heavy pressure. They in turn are putting ​more ​and more pressure on the Saudis, increasing their campaign of missile and drone attacks," one of the Yemeni ​officials said.

Saudi Arabia's 1,200-km (745-mile) East-West Pipeline, which links its Gulf ‌oil fields to the Red Sea, has been the Kingdom's principal export route while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted by six months of war.

Since the pipeline was shut after Friday's attack, traders say a prolonged closure could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply. Riyadh has not said when operations might resume.

The new Houthi presence in the Bab el-Mandeb, or "Gate of Tears", the strait at the mouth of the Red Sea, could further jeopardise that crucial export route.

Oil prices have risen since last week to levels unseen since May. Brent crude oil futures rose above $108 a barrel on Tuesday, while the politically sensitive average retail price of diesel in the U.S. hit a new all-time high of nearly $6.27 a gallon.

The United Nations ‌Security Council will discuss the worsening crisis in the Bab el-Mandeb on Tuesday afternoon, two French diplomats said.

Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015. The conflict had largely quietened ​under a ceasefire in recent years, but fighting reignited this month, with the Houthis ​pushing back forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.

The United States, which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, now faces a dilemma: whether ‌to stand by and risk new threats to the global economy, or ​offer military support to the Saudis and risk being ​pulled into another costly theatre of war.

Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi in Cairo on Tuesday. A statement from the Egyptian presidency after the meeting said the leaders stressed the need to ensure freedom and security of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb and the Red Sea.

The crown prince met the U.S. regional ​military commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, in Jeddah on Monday, and phoned President ‌Donald Trump last week seeking military support, which so far has been limited to intelligence aid.

title: Georgia mayor, 23, ousted 10 months after making history as state’s youngest mayor
description: Jayden Williams, 23, was removed by the Stockbridge City Council after allegations involving public funds and communications with an 18-year-old student.
fullText:
Georgia's youngest elected mayor was removed from office just 10 months after taking the job following allegations that he misused city funds and exchanged sexually suggestive messages and images with an 18-year-old high school student.

Jayden Williams, who recently turned 23, was impeached by the Stockbridge City Council in the city south of Atlanta after taking office in January.

"The City of Stockbridge confirms that the City Council has taken formal action concerning the Office of Mayor," the city said in a statement on Sunday. "The Mayor has been removed from office."

Williams was accused of using his city purchasing card for more than $4,000 in personal expenses, including restaurant meals, clothing, haircuts and a movie, according to Fox 5 Atlanta. He reportedly spent $2,600 on gas and used a city vehicle for personal purposes.

Massachusetts Mayor Charged With Wire Fraud In $1.5M Covid Relief Scheme

The spending was reported after city workers noticed unusual transactions involving public funds and immediately notified management and the city's legal team.

According to Williams' testimony, he did not intend to use city funds and later repaid the money, Fox 5 reported. He further claimed the city-issued card looked similar to his personal card and said he later replaced the cards to avoid future confusion, the outlet reported.

Former Democratic Mayor Of State Capital City Pleads Guilty For Role In Six-figure Real Estate Bribery Scheme

Separately, Williams was accused of exchanging sexually suggestive messages and explicit images with an 18-year-old male high school student.

A police report noted that Williams did not commit any criminal violations because the student was considered an adult under Georgia law. However, police referred the matter for administrative review over potential policy and ethical concerns about an elected official's interactions with a student in what investigators described as a city-affiliated mentorship program, Fox 5 reported.

In a statement, Williams previously said he met the individual before taking office and that the student never participated in the city's "Mayor for a Day" program, which Williams described as not a mentorship program.

Ex-mayor Found Liable For Alleged Sexual Assaults Of 7 Women, Ordered To Pay $13M

"The individual was 18 years old at the time of our communication, meaning we were both adults. I met this individual on November 30, 2025, and our online communication occurred before I was sworn into office in January 2026," he said.

Williams became the youngest mayor in Georgia history after campaigning for the position while still attending Clark Atlanta University.

He was subsequently stripped of certain official privileges on July 17 as the investigation unfolded but was never criminally charged in connection with the alleged conduct.
