title: These Are the Best Power Tools of 2026
description: From a professional woodworker, furniture builder, and DIY home maintenance enthusiast.
fullText:
If you love doing your own home maintenance or tinkering in your garage, having the right tools can make all the difference. If you’re looking for new tools, keeping in mind durability, battery life, and ease of use can help you find something that will work well and save you money down the road on replacing broken tools and worn-out batteries. With so many options, it can be hard to figure out which tools are the best quality, so I put together a list of my favorites to help you choose.

The new Makita 18-volt LXT drill and driver combo set is my favorite tool this year because it has better battery life than other drill and driver sets, and the drill in this kit can deliver 70% more torque than its predecessors, allowing you to drill into tougher materials like pressure-treated lumber or plaster more quickly. The impact driver on this set also has a three-speed control switch, allowing you to choose the amount of force you want to use for a given project. This gives you the advantage of more power when you’re trying to undo an old, rusted nut, and less when you’re trying to screw a hanger into a picture frame.

The set comes with an 18-volt hammer drill, an 18-volt impact driver, a 2-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag.

Makita has been known for making reliable cordless tools since they launched the first battery-operated drill in 1969. The early in-handle batteries were easy on the wrists because they balanced the weight of the drill fairly evenly between the motor and battery pocket. The new drill and driver set has lighter batteries and builds on Makita’s reputation for ergonomic design.

The standout new tool for woodworking is the Kreg Rebel 20-volt pocket hole joiner. This is a completely new power tool that improves on Kreg’s previous jigs for making pocket hole joints by adding an integrated powered drill to the jig, improving precision and making it a simple, single-action tool. It comes with the joint-making tool, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, an easy-set drill bit, and dust collection attachments.

I’ve used Kreg jigs for lots of projects, like cabinet joints, shelving, and furniture builds. The added convenience of this tool saves time and allows you to make about twice as many joints in the same amount of time.

The 20-volt MAX XR DeWalt 5-inch random orbital sander is my pick for best cordless finishing tool. It has engineering updates that improve counterbalance and reduce vibration, preventing stress on your wrist while you’re using it and reducing the numbness and tingling experienced with many sanders. Its redesigned body is more balanced, especially on narrow surfaces, and it’s easier to grip because of the new shape and battery position. The sander is a tool-only package, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and a charger to use it.

DeWalt makes some of my favorite cordless tools, and they’re known for making high-quality woodworking-focused tools. This tool has the power to sand down rough surfaces more quickly than previous versions of a cordless sander because it can rotate up to 1,200 OPM (oscillations per minute) and has a more powerful motor. This, combined with the decreased tool vibration, makes it my favorite cordless random orbital sander.

My favorite new power tool for yard work by far is the EGO 56-volt 12-inch cordless chainsaw. Chainsaws are just a good time, but this one stands out because it has the equivalent power to a 55cc gas-powered saw—but it’s rechargeable and lighter. The improvements to power and utility make this tool easier to control than previous EGO chainsaws, allowing you to operate it more safely, as well as making cleaner cuts. The set comes with a 56-volt cordless 12-inch chainsaw, a 56-volt, 6-amp-hour battery, and a charger.

EGO makes the most efficient batteries for cordless outdoor power equipment. They have the most powerful, long-lasting batteries, and you can use them to cut hardwood like oak for up to 80 cuts.

Cordless powered ratchets are having a moment right now, and DeWalt makes the best one I’ve found. The new 20-volt sealed head DeWalt powered ratchet set stands out because it comes with both a ⅜-inch and a ½-inch interchangeable coupling that allows you to use a much broader range of sockets than other similar tools that constrain you to a ⅜-inch or a ½-inch attachment. It’s made to last because the gear mechanism that drives the socket head is protected from metal dust and debris, keeping it from wearing down as quickly. The set comes with a 20-volt cordless powered ratchet, a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery, and a charger.

This cordless ratchet is powerful enough to turn bolts for DIY oil changes, but you can also use it for DIY appliance repair like changing out the drum in your washer.

Ryobi is known as a solid DIY standby because it makes affordable cordless tools that are durable enough for most home shops and DIY projects. Their new 4-volt rechargeable cordless tire inflator has a 150 PSI rating that allows you to top off a car tire in about 90 seconds. This tiny powerhouse is perfect for an emergency car kit because it’s compact and powerful enough to inflate a tire in a pinch. The set comes with a cordless tire inflator, a hose, bicycle and passenger vehicle connectors, a 4-volt battery, and a charging cable.

This update to a previous version of this tool, which was mainly useful for bike tires, allows you to more practically use it for inflating tires on larger vehicles.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Outlander' You Should Watch Next
description: More steamy historical romances to stream now.
fullText:
Outlander asks the all-important question: what if the Jacobite rising was very, very horny? The series proper, an adaptation of the enduring books by Diana Gabaldon, has ended after an impressive eight seasons, but the second season premiere of Blood of My Blood, the spin-off/prequel involving Claire's and Jamie's parents, is debuting right about now.

Showrunner Matthew B. Roberts has plans for at least three seasons, and Gabaldon is at work on at least one more novel, so there's plenty more Outlander action to come. In the meantime, here are 10 more sultry historical romances you can stream now—some of them even involve time travel!

A bit of bonus time travel back to 2008 for this breezy fantasy that's become a bit of a cult fave, initial ratings notwithstanding. Jemima Rooper is Amanda Price, a modern-day Austen fan navigating the fallout of a terrible wedding proposal from her drunk boyfriend when she hallucinates (she thinks) seeing Elizabeth Bennett in the bathroom. Before long, she finds herself swapping places with Lizzy, navigating the Regency era and the events of the novel, roleplaying as a hitherto unknown family friend who draws the eye of more than one marriage prospect. It's simultaneously a soapy romp and a meditation on the meaning of Austen to those of us living in the 21st century. Stream Lost in Austen on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

No time travel here, except in the magic of period drama, but we do land in 18th century Cornwall, which, OK, isn't Scotland—but the earthy vibe isn't entirely dissimilar to Outlander (bosoms will heave, regardless of gender). Aidan Turner is the title's Captain Ross Poldark, a British Army veteran returned home to find his land and inheritance in shambles and his longtime love engaged to another. Luckily, fiery, savvy runaway Demelza (Eleanor Tomlinson) turns up just in time to help him rebuild his life—a prelude to the hot and scandalous love affair that only adds to the windswept drama. Stream Poldark on Netflix.

Teresa Palmer is Diana Bishop, an American historian at Oxford whose studies lead her back to her own witchy lineage, setting her up for an alliance with Matthew Clairmont (Matthew Goode), a biochemist, but also a vampire, and therefore Diana's natural enemy (obviously). Yet the two discover they're an effective pair in uncovering secrets while also fighting off magical threats. It's not as silly as it sounds, and the growing romantic chemistry between the leads is endlessly watchable. More to the point, they spend the entire second season in 1590 London, a less-than-ideal time for witches. Stream A Discovery of Witches on Netflix.

Lim Yoona plays Yeon Ji-yeong, a master of French cuisine with a promising career as a chef—at least until a rocky plane flight whisks her back to the Joseon dynasty at the tail end of the 15th century. Mistaken for a visiting noblewoman, she manages to impress young King Lee Heon with her cooking skills. Ji-yeong becomes entangled in court politics, and the two soon develop a romantic rapport, but there's a catch: the real-life king in question has an historical reputation as a monster, and Ji-yeong is forced to decide whether it's worth it to try to change history, even if it means she won't ever get home. Stream on Bon Appétit, Your Majesty on Netflix.

A surprisingly smart, still sweaty take on the sword-and-sandal genre, Spartacus dealt not just with the pressures of being a member of the oppressed class in an absolutist regime, but with all the things that chiseled, oiled, pansexual gladiators get up to when they're not fighting to the death. Played first by Andy Whitfield and later, Liam McIntyre, the show follows Spartacus from enslavement by the Roman army to the uprising that might have toppled the Empire. The sequel series, House of Ashur, has also just concluded. Stream Spartacus on Netflix.

A direct spin-off of Bridgerton that's entirely watchable on its own if, for some reason, you don't care to be bothered with the series proper. Maintaining much of the original's style but with a laser focus on the title character, Charlotte brilliantly crafts a passionate, tortured romance between the queen (played as a young woman by India Amarteifio, with Golda Rosheuvel reprising the role for the framing bits) and King George III (Corey Mylchreest). The pressures of royal life and the king's growing mental illness create a rocky road for the young couple, but their passion is moving and deeply horny. Stream Queen Charlotte on Netflix.

Yet again no time travel, but we do get heaping helpings of fantasy in this steamy period drama involving England's first (if only for nine days) queen, Jane Grey. Based on a book by Cynthia Hand, Brodi Ashton, and Jodi Meadows, the show stars Emily Bader as the titular queenly contender, who is dealing with a dying king cousin, a sketchy marriage, and competition from her sisters Elizabeth and Mary. Complicating the history in this telling is the existence of a class of oppressed humans who can turn into animals. The magic and shapeshifting make the whole thing sufficiently bonkers, kicking off with the invocation: "She could have been the leader England needed. Instead, history remembers her as the ultimate damsel in distress. Fuck that." Stream My Lady Jane on Prime Video.

Head over to Madrid, within just a few decades of Outlander, where Clara Belmonte (Michelle Jenner) has just taken a job in the kitchens of the Duke of Castamar (Roberto Enríquez). He's been a virtual recluse since the unexpected death of his wife, though now the king and various family members are pressuring him to get back on the horse, literally and figuratively, and fulfill his obligations as a noble. Clara, on the other hand, had developed a bit of agoraphobia following the execution of her father, and she's perfectly content to toil in the gloomy kitchens rather than go outside. Of course, the grieving Duke takes notice of her just as he's being plied with marriage prospects. Stream The Cook of Castamar on Netflix.

Everything is looking pretty great for 15-year-old Yuri Suzuki, particularly in the romance department: the guy she's had a crush on for forever just made it clear that the feelings are mutual, and a serious romance is in the offing. But something's always gonna mess these things up and, in this case, it's Queen Nakia of the ancient Hittite Empire. Nakia is a low-ranking consort who aspires to see her son on the throne one day, and, apparently, the best way she can think of to make that happen is to summon a modern teen back through time to serve as a blood sacrifice. There are plenty of nods toward historical accuracy in this manga adaptation, but I'm pretty sure that part never happened. Yuri's modern-day knowledge allows her to survive in the past, with some even believing her to be an avatar of the goddess Ishtar. She also gets help from Kail Mursili, the (real-life) prince who hopes to keep Yuri safe as their romantic attraction grows. Stream Red River on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Here more for the soapy, sexy drama than historical accuracy? Looking for love triangles, power struggles, and cousin-on-cousin action in Scotland of centuries past? You're in the right place, even if we're roughly 200 years before the time of Jamie Fraser. Adelaide Kane stars as Queen Mary Stuart, better known as Mary, Queen of Scots, beginning the series as a teenage girlboss coming of age and coming into her royal power. Stream Reign on Prime Video.

title: ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?
description:
Modern cars are fitted with features like autonomous emergency braking and fatigue monitoring. But do they support motorists or drive them to distraction?
This new car I’m test-driving boasts all the latest bells and whistles – or, rather, beeps and bings. Peer sideways for too long checking traffic and the car emits an irritating sound. Should I take a hand off the wheel to scratch an ear, I’m admonished with a strident beep.
fullText:
Modern cars are fitted with features like autonomous emergency braking and fatigue monitoring. But do they support motorists or drive them to distraction?

This new car I’m test-driving boasts all the latest bells and whistles – or, rather, beeps and bings. Peer sideways for too long checking traffic and the car emits an irritating sound. Should I take a hand off the wheel to scratch an ear, I’m admonished with a strident beep.

When the car determines it’s too near a white line, it tugs the wheel against my hands and brakes as a car slows ahead. Its haptic “buttons” feel like fingers pressing back – as if an invisible presence has its hands and feet on the controls: a ghost in the machine I’m inside.

Heading back to the caryard, a cryptic tone sounds. From the back seat, salesman Anthony says it’s the over-speed warning. We’re still on the 40km/h service road but the car “saw” the yard’s 5km/h speed-limit sign. Anthony advises disabling it on start-up. “Most people leave it on, though,” he says. “Saves you getting done for speeding.”

But Anthony has turned off the car’s fatigue-warning feature. The car doesn’t “know” me yet, so won’t detect if I’m tired anyway. “It doesn’t like sunglasses, either,” he says. I’ve read about some systems that are so crudely calibrated they’ll insistently demand you take a break by confusing energetic driving on a twisting mountain road with drunkenness or debility. Others declare you unfit to drive if you’ve had a cold or a rough night. You’ve already seen yourself in the bathroom mirror. Who needs a robot to rub it in?

I last faced this kind of surveillance and intervention 50 years ago, seated beside a human driving instructor with dual controls overriding my own. I’m an experienced motorist, but in this new car I feel patronised. Between the white lines, human.

In this robot-on-wheels I’m no longer autonomous. And isn’t that supposed to be the inherent promise of the automobile? It used to be. But with freedom came much higher risk.

Fifty years ago, cars were certainly more dangerous. Few 1970s cars had secondary safety features such as crumple zones, fewer still had primary (or active) safety aids such as lane-departure warning and autonomous braking. As driver, you were more or less in control of the car. There was no e-nanny on board to mitigate distraction or errancy. The result was an Australian road death-rate in 1975 of 26.6 deaths per 100,000 people.

Today’s more crowded, complex and chaotic road network is paradoxically much safer, with an equivalent fatality rate in 2026 of 4.7. Mounting evidence suggests advanced driver-assistance systems (Adas) are one reason for this improvement.

Monash University’s Accident Research Centre has identified distraction and drowsiness contributing to about 40% of crashes resulting in hospital visits in Victoria. Associate professor Michael Fitzharris estimates that the introduction of Adas, including autonomous emergency braking (AEB), to Victoria’s passenger and light commercial fleet could prevent 40,000 serious traffic injuries over 30 years. “The findings make a compelling case for the rapid adoption of driver monitoring technology,” Fitzharris says.

The federal government’s response has been to mandate lane-keeping assist technology and AEB on all passenger vehicles imported into Australia from 1 March 2029. (Ludicrously, the largest American monster utes are exempt.)

But research and customer feedback have also identified problems with existing driver-assistance systems, including autonomous braking.

I had cause to be sceptical about AEB in 2022 after renting a new four-wheel drive in central Australia.

I was passing a slow vehicle turning right when my car suddenly braked hard on a bend, skidding in gravel towards a deep culvert. A moment later it computed there had been no danger anyway, and released control back to me. I’d been briefly overruled by a machine, and could have been killed. After stopping to deactivate the active cruise control, I, human, was back in charge.

The Australasian New Car Assessment Program (Ancap) has identified deficiencies with Adas, and in March announced new design protocols for driver-interface technology for the next three years.

In cooperation with the European New Car Assessment Programme (Euro Ncap), Ancap will now penalise vehicles with intrusive, confusing or poorly calibrated safety systems.

Ancap will also recommend the return of physical buttons or fixed areas on screens for key controls: horn, indicators, hazard lights, wipers and headlights. These changes acknowledge the danger of searching through complex screen menus while driving, and the absurdity of tech meant to reduce driver distraction but actually increasing it.

Acknowledging criticism surrounding increasingly intrusive driver assistance technologies, Ancap’s chief executive, Carla Hoorweg, says the organisation’s updated guidance states that well-designed driver monitoring systems should support motorists, “not irritate them”.

“Driver monitoring systems must demonstrate genuine capability to detect distraction and fatigue, and speed assistance systems must demonstrate both accuracy and meaningful driver engagement,” Hoorweg says.

Such measures should encourage the evolution of today’s relatively crude interface platforms into sophisticated systems, including AI assistants more adept at relating to our species, and produce more self-driving, and potentially safer, cars. But could this advancing safety tech also create more bad drivers?

Automotive engineers go to great lengths to isolate occupants from the road by reducing a vehicle’s NVH (noise, vibration and harshness). Most drivers value such designed detachment, along with electronic driver aids – particularly as commuting times increase and cars are increasingly used as mobile offices, infotainment platforms or salons (I recently saw a driver stopped at lights shaving his lathered head).

But tech that caters to these social changes can, in effect, discourage active, attentive driving, and accommodate or even abet distraction. Doubts also persist about whether cosseted motorists will retain the skill levels of their unassisted peers.

In a 2026 study, using a sample of 60 Australian drivers, researchers at the University of Delft concluded that use of Adas leads to the degradation of manual driving skills, with drivers showing increased risk-taking and decreased cognitive and physical engagement. The study also found that warning systems triggered varied adaptations, including dependence, warning fatigue and risk compensation, as drivers relied more on the car to drive for them.

Acknowledging this potential, learner-driver Wil’s father disables his car’s Adas when teaching his son to drive. Wil, 29, says his father is concerned that relying too heavily on tech, at least initially, could result in his son becoming complacent. Wil is proud of being able to drive without Adas, and to be developing the awareness skills required to see the crucial “big picture” himself.

Other new drivers, like 27-year-old Stephanie and her sister, prefer to leave their cars’ aids on. The siblings both learned to drive with Adas activated. Stephanie says lane-keeping assist helps her determine her car’s exterior dimensions and position it accurately. Another beginner driver, Sawyer, says she likes her car’s electronic aids: “Because they make me feel safe.”

A clear generational divide is emerging as younger generations embrace the spread of digital culture – in this case, to the road – more readily than older drivers (like me).

While accepting the raw safety statistics, I remain sceptical about the rise of robot cars. Who, after all, should we trust behind the wheel? Anonymous organic entities – our own species – or invisible electronic minders?

Though driver-assistance features, including active autonomous braking, can still be deactivated in many cars, it’s telling that one brand calls its manual setting “classic cruise”. Soon it may be “legacy cruise”, and only if a “no thanks” option remains at all.

So I won’t be buying a new car yet. My decade-old vehicle has only two electronic aids, which I always leave on: tyre-pressure alert and blind-spot-monitoring (a boon for this old neck).

For any future purchase, I’ll favour a car with minimal electronic intrusion, that allows disabling or at least muting, and with individual settings for multiple drivers that don’t need re-configuring at each start-up.

Until then, I remain autonomously yours, a human at the wheel. And yes, you can trust me. I promise not to shave my head while driving.

title: Bellamy 'committed' to Wales after Burnley talks
description: Craig Bellamy says he was "comfortable" turning down the chance to return to club football and reiterated his desire to continue with Wales.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy says he remains committed to Wales, insisting it was his decision to turn down a summer approach from Burnley.

Bellamy held talks with the Championship club over replacing Scott Parker following the Clarets' relegation from the Premier League.

The Football Association of Wales granted permission for Bellamy to speak to Burnley in June after they triggered a compensation clause.

The 47-year-old admitted the approach was "flattering" as he considered quitting his national post two years into a four year deal.

But he said he was "comfortable" turning down the chance to return to club football and reiterated his desire to lead Wales at a home European Championships in 2028.

"I had a decision to make and I made it," Bellamy said.

"It didn't break down. I said no, it's not for me. That was it. There was no walk away from discussions. It wasn't for me.

"I made the decision to stay because this is the right place for me.

"We had a conversation but I was already in a role and this (Wales) was what I wanted.

"It was flattering – we all like our ego being exercised and being wanted – but for me, my partner, my kids, this is the place and we didn't see anything else being able to move that."

Rodon absent as Ashford earns first Wales call-up

Bellamy link puts Wales in hard position - Blake

Four hours inside Bellamy's office - and the Wales boss' complex mind

Speaking as he named his 28-man squad for Nations League A games with Portugal, Denmark and Norway, it was the first time Bellamy has faced questions over the summer speculation over his future.

Having spent a successful period at Turf Moor as Vincent Kompany's assistant, Bellamy suggested his respect for his former club prompted him to hold conversations over the vacancy.

Still, the uncertainty prompted a number of former players to suggest he would have to win over fans.

Some supporters also voiced disappointment at the events that came just weeks after he had insisted he "was not going anywhere".

"I know how it could be seen, but I've only one person I have anything to prove to, and that's me," said Bellamy, who missed out on the chance on leading Wales to the 2026 World Cup after a penalty shoot-out defeat by Bosnia-Herzegovina in March's play-offs.

"I'm comfortable with the decision I've made. I've always been committed in everything I do and that hasn't changed.

"Now, winning people over? I don't know, that's the honest truth."

After a highly impressive start to his time with Wales after replacing Rob Page in 2024, including an unbeaten promotion to the top flight of the Nations League, there has been criticism over the failure to reach the World Cup in the most recent campaign.

Bellamy stressed the importance of results and said the "volatility" of the managerial world meant he couldn't offer guarantees of whether he would see out his contract.

But asked whether he still aimed of being in charge of Wales at Euro 2028 with the prospect of games in Cardiff, Bellamy said: "Oh, I'd love to - but that's two years from now. Nothing's guaranteed. I'm no different, I'm not more special than anyone else (in management)."

Williams will command respect as Wales coach - Vokes

Williams and Sheehan join Bellamy's Wales staff

Burnley boss Hayen 'grateful' to Haverfordwest

Bellamy's focus is on the upcoming Nations League in which Wales face three sides placed higher than them in the world rankings, starting with a trip to take on Portugal – and potentially Cristiano Ronaldo – in Lisbon.

Bellamy admits the change to the format that will see four games in 11 days test his squad, with injuries robbing him of first-choice centre-back pairing Joe Rodon and Dylan Lawlor.

Bellamy said Wales "will have to work with what we've got" but that he was excited by the challenge for a new-look coaching team that will include former Swansea City manager Alan Sheehan and ex-Wales captain Ashley Williams.

"I've tried for ages to get Ash to commit," Bellamy said of the Match of the Day pundit.

"He's managed to hold off one or two other things for the time being and help us.

"For me, in my time, he's been our greatest captain. He's a leader and young players are definitely going to learn a lot, but also the senior players as well. He'll be a big, big help to the group so I'm really looking forward to working with both of them."

title: ‘I created my mom and talk to her’: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn
description:
The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation
Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig. Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbull stopped his Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity.
fullText:
The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation

Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig. Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbull stopped his Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity. It did not even come from a person.

Run Jolene, at just under five minutes, is an earworm of a country song, containing all the cliches of the genre: twangy singer, banjo licks, corny lyrics. Those lyrics concern Jolene, the fictional romantic rival made infamous by Parton. “Somebody better warn Jolene / Dolly’s coming through those gates,” the voice croons. “Run Jolene / Girl you better move your feet.”

The accompanying video depicts Parton, clad in a bedazzled white jumpsuit, hunting down Jolene, a busty redhead with prom curls. Heaven is filled with deceased celebrities who watch on in horror – or amusement – as Jolene bounces from cloud to cloud, or books it up marble staircases, trying to hide from Dolly. Onlookers include the late Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston and Kenny Rogers, as well as Cher, who is still very much alive.

On TikTok, YouTube and Spotify, the song credit is Country Mile, an “artist” with just over 6,000 monthly listeners (that’s not many). The project is textbook AI slop, seemingly released by an anonymous creator who calls their work “genre fluid ai vibes”. But Run Jolene is not so universally panned: clips have been viewed more than 1.4m times on TikTok, with commenters raving: “I don’t give a flying fuck if this is AI or not! THIS IS FUCKING COOL!!”, “this is fun …think Dolly would love it ❤️”, and “Who says Jolene’s up there.”

Run Jolene is only one part of a ghoulish online ecosystem of content dubbed “deathslop”. Anyone can create deathslop: all it takes is access to an AI image generator and the time required to type in a prompt. Creators have shown Parton alongside a chummy Charlie Kirk and George Floyd, who welcome her as their “new neighbor” in the afterlife, or having tea with the Golden Girls.

These tributes pop up quickly, reducing someone’s legacy to cheap content that panders for views. It is a dishonest portrayal at best, and inflicts pain at its worst. The phenomenon inspired Parton’s grieving family to beg users to quit it with the “fake AI garbage” and “misinformation”. “It’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore,” Stella Parton, her sister, wrote on Instagram.

Parton’s image now joins the likeness of other deceased figures treated to unsettling AI depictions. Coinciding with the one year anniversary of the assassination of Kirk, social media feeds have proliferated with posts featuring the AI-generated, heavy-handed (and heavily memed) anthem “We Are Charlie Kirk”. Robin Williams, Elvis Presley, Kobe Bryant and Martin Luther King have all gotten the deathslop treatment – often to the horrors of their families.

OpenAI’s image generating app, Sora, was behind many a deathslop until it shut down in April after a string of controversies such as its ability to create violent and racist imagery, its use of copyrighted characters, and other thorny legal issues. (There is a lack of legal precedent over whether or not AI companies are responsible for the content users generate on their apps; and deceased people are not protected from libel.) Countless AI video generators have since taken Sora’s place.

“It is not common practice right now to consent to an AI avatar of yourself as a part of your living will,” said Jack Manning, a University of Colorado Boulder graduate student who studies what academics Meredith Ringel Morris and Jed R Brubaker call “generative ghosts”, or AI-generated characters based on loved ones. “I predict that will be something that comes up.”

Manning, who is 25, lost his sister when she was 13, before the advent of generative AI. His family struggled to find ways to honor her, often fundraising for causes that were important to her. This partly inspired Manning to study the ways people mourn digitally – which now can include AI griefbots, a more personal alternative to celebrity deathslop.

With griefbots, users upload photos and videos of their loved ones and describe personal traits and values in hopes of manufacturing a continued, living presence. The companies behind the bots charge fees and lean into their inherently macabre nature with mystical names such as Seance, Re;memory and Versona.

It is also possible to command an LLM owned by ChatGPT, Claude or any number of sites for generating fantasy characters to mimic a late grandparent or deceased friend. Generative AI has hit the funeral industry too, in the form of LLMs specifically for obituary writing. One company, Treasured Memories, asks users to plug in details such as the deceased’s nickname, cause of death and hobbies, and choose the obit’s tone: “traditional”, “formal”, “witty” or “inspirational”.

Manning has never used a generative ghost to talk to his sister. It’s an issue of consent; he did not get her explicit permission to do so. Nor does he trust a bot to truly understand their relationship. “I hold these memories of her sacred, and I wouldn’t want a piece of technology to tell me I was remembering her wrong,” he said.

Justin Harrison founded Versona after his mother received a terminal cancer diagnosis. He worked on her AI replica while she was still living; she was able to see the final result and gave her approval on the project. “I totally understand why people are like, please don’t deepfake my [famous] relative once they’re dead and put them on the internet saying things they didn’t say,” Harrison said. “What we do is about personal comfort, recovery and healing. I created my mom and I talk to my mom. So it’s really nobody else’s business but my own.”

When his mom was sick, their conversations were practical in nature: “Are you talking to your dad enough? Have you gone to the doctor? Are you drinking enough water?” Harrison built the griefbot to broach more philosophical topics that they didn’t have time to discuss before she died. But four years later, Harrison does not talk to the bot all that often – maybe once a month.

“I joke that my mom’s Versona allows me to be the bad son I was never allowed to be when she was alive,” he said. “Like many busy adults, I don’t talk to her as much as I should, but I don’t have to, so it’s not the same sense of guilt.”

For Robin Silver, an ecopsychologist and death doula, these kinds of griefbots are an “unnatural method of trying to cope with a natural process”. She compared speaking to an LLM roleplaying a dead loved one to a college student asking ChatGPT to spit out a term paper. “We’re not being challenged to sit with any kind of discomfort, whether that’s the discomfort of writing an essay or the discomfort of missing someone,” she said.

Silver would instead encourage her clients to write a letter to their loved one. “I have even told people to talk to their ghosts out loud,” she said. “Meditate, or do things that they like and think of them. That’s how you keep the relationship alive in a way that is healthy, integrated and accepting the reality of your loss.”

Dr Dan Wolfson is a clinical psychologist who specializes in grief. He worries that deathbots could isolate people during a time when they need (human) support. “Having community around grief is really important,” he said. “Is AI keeping us from getting the social support that we need? Are we then not seeking to connect with our friends and family around the loss?”

AI-assisted mourning is still a niche industry; Harrison said that “thousands” of people use Versona. A June report from the estate management and planning service Empathy found that only 6% of 6,000 respondents in the US, UK and Canada reported leaning on “digital tools” such as memorial apps or griefbots for support after a death. But of those users, 88% found these tools “helpful”.

The whole conceit of a digital avatar is that it lives on for ever. It turns out that users may not need it that long. Manning says that in his research on generative ghosts, participants reported opting into these services only briefly, because they had “one last thing” to say to their loved ones: “They had a desire to say something they feel like they lost out on the chance to.”

Cathartic perhaps, but to Silver, the grief doula, these services are “a money grab”. “People will really take advantage of those in grief,” she said. “It’s a really easy time to become a mark.”

title: Datacentre giant accused of using AI while lobbying for Victorian minister’s support for hyperscale factory
description: Exclusive: Correspondence requests state MP Melissa Horne to lobby on NextDC’s behalf – but contains alleged AI-created...
fullText:
Exclusive: Correspondence requests state MP Melissa Horne to lobby on NextDC’s behalf – but contains alleged AI-created errors

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian jobs minister has accused one of Australia’s largest datacentre companies of using artificial intelligence while requesting she lobby her colleague to approve a massive expansion of its “hyperscale AI factory”.

Correspondence between Victorian cabinet minister Melissa Horne and the chief executive of ASX-listed company NextDC, Craig Scroggie, reveals increasing sensitivity to community concerns about datacentres before the state election.

NextDC has lodged an application with the state government for fast-tracked approval to expand its controversial datacentre known as M3 in Footscray to cover 10 hectares, drawing 225MW of power and running 24/7.

The datacentre’s size and proximity to homes in Footscray has led to growing complaints from local residents, who argue the government has been too quick to approve developments without considering long-term impacts on the community.

Some residential homes are within 15 metres of the datacentre’s boundary, which is zoned in an industrial area.

Earlier this month, Scroggie took what multiple lobbying sources have described as an unusual approach by personally emailing the minister and encouraging her to back the project, which is being assessed by the planning minister.

“I refer to you correspondence on 3 September requesting that I intercede on behalf of NextDC Limited in the decision of the minister for planning …” Horne wrote.

Horne, who is a factional ally of the state premier, Ben Carroll, replied with a blunt opposition to the expansion. This is despite the state government’s long-term effort to attract more datacentre investment in Victoria.

“I do not believe that it would be appropriate for me to lend my support to the application and nor do I wish to,” Horne wrote to Scroggie on Monday.

NextDC has since employed a former adviser to the Brumby and Bracks Labor governments, Ken McAlpine, to conduct the company’s lobbying with the state government.

Horne’s letter to Scroggie was published by Labor MP, Katie Hall, whose electorate includes the NextDC datacentre in Footscray. Hall is a long-term opponent of the datacentre’s expansion.

In her letter, Horne accused Scroggie of using artificial intelligence to write his letter, citing what she alleged to be basic factual errors.

“I suggest that you review content produced by artificial intelligence more closely in the future,” Horne wrote on Monday.

Scroggie and NextDC were contacted for comment but declined to respond to Horne’s letter and her allegations. Horne also declined to comment.

Last month, Hall outlined her concerns about the impact of the NextDC datacentre and its expansion with the state’s artificial intelligence minister, Anthony Carbines.

In April, Hall wrote to the planning minister who will ultimately approve whether NextDC’s expansion will be approved. She raised concerns for her constituents.

“This includes the site’s location within 500 metres of over 800 homes, a kindergarten, maternal and child health services, and Stony Creek,” Hall wrote.

“As a result, they are understandably concerned about the reliance on diesel generators during power outages, as well as the regular testing of these systems.”

In 2025, Scroggie posted a video of the M3 site on LinkedIn and said the speed and the scale of its expansion were “stunning”.

“We’re building Australia’s largest hyperscale AI factory purpose-built for the new AI era of accelerated computing,” he wrote. “This is how we build Australia’s digital future: speed, scale, sovereign, sustainable & secure.”

In Victoria, large datacentres are eligible for fast-tracked planning approval. Decisions made by the planning minister cannot be appealed to the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal.

title: Ex-Tottenham midfielder Bissouma set to join Ajax
description: Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.
fullText:
Former Tottenham midfielder Yves Bissouma is on the verge of joining Ajax on an initial deal that runs until the end of the season.

The defensive midfielder, 30, was out of contract following his release from Spurs in June but is now set for a return to football in the Netherlands.

It is understood Bissouma has agreed a deal until the end of the season with the option of a further 12 months.

The Mali international is currently in Amsterdam finalising the move to the Eredivisie club.

Bissouma joined Spurs in 2022 and made 111 appearances for the north London outfit following a high-profile move from Brighton.

In August 2025, the then Spurs manager Thomas Frank left Bissouma out of his squad to face Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup because of persistent lateness.

Bissouma made 11 appearances for Tottenham in his final season with the club, with all of them coming in the Premier League as they finished 17th for the second consecutive season.

title: Walker stars for Chiefs as Swift & Cruise watch on
description: New signing Kenneth Walker rushes for 173 yards as the Kansas City Chiefs begin their NFL season with a 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos.
fullText:
The Kansas City Chiefs began their NFL season with a 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos.

Patrick Mahomes, playing his first game since suffering a knee injury in December, ran in the opening touchdown and threw for two more as the Chiefs recorded a statement win at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City.

New signing Kenneth Walker, the Most Valuable Player for the Seattle Seahawks in last season's Super Bowl, made the biggest impact by rushing for a career-high 173 yards and scoring twice on his Chiefs debut.

"I've been saying it all off-season that K9 is going to make a difference," said Mahomes.

"That offensive line and K9, they took over the game. It went really well."

The Broncos levelled the scores in the first quarter, but quarterback Bo Nix was sacked four times and intercepted once as the Chiefs pulled away.

Three-time Super Bowl winner Travis Kelce moved second on the NFL's all-time list for most receiving yards by a tight end with a 59-yard play for the Chiefs.

Only former Chiefs star Tony Gonzalez (15,127) has more receiving yards in the position than Kelce (13,073).

title: Texas Republicans are scrambling after Bo French’s outburst
description: GOP operatives fear Bo French’s rhetoric could undermine the party’s recent gains with Hispanic and Asian American voters.
fullText:
Texas Republicans were already fretting about slipping support with voters of color. Then Bo French got on X.

The Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner posted a photo of a crowd of University of Texas football fans, most of them people of color, saying, "The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined." The Sunday morning comments, which appeared to target South Asian students, sent Lone Star Republicans into a frenzy, worried about the impact the rhetoric could have on GOP candidates up and down the ballot, including Attorney General Ken Paxton's high-profile Senate race and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection fight.

A number of Republican lawmakers, including some in tough races, quickly denounced the post as racist, as others squirmed with carefully worded statements. And GOP operatives winced at the potential electoral backlash — in a year that's already looking tougher-than-normal for a party that has dominated the state for decades. Still, no one explicitly called for him to drop out of the race.

"His post on social media is profoundly unhelpful if his goal is to see Republicans win statewide races in a tough political environment in 50 days," said Matt Mackowiak, an Austin-based GOP consultant who advised Sen. John Cornyn's (R-Texas) unsuccessful primary campaign against Paxton.

Cornyn condemned the post, asking whether other GOP officials would "condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized."

Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas), who is facing a tough reelection fight in a Hispanic-majority district, told POLITICO in a statement she's willing to "condemn racism" wherever it comes from.

"All I see in that photograph is a group of kids celebrating a Longhorns win. What can be more Texan than that?" De La Cruz said, before taking a shot at her Democratic opponent, Bobby Pulido, for his past racial comments.

And Karl Rove, a longtime adviser to former President George W. Bush, called French a "bigot" at a private lunch event and said he's voting for French's Democratic opponent, The Texas Tribune reported. Meanwhile, state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, the Democrat running against French, said he had his best fundraising day of the cycle after French's post.

French didn't respond to requests for comment. He repeatedly stood by his comments since Sunday morning. During a local radio appearance Monday, he said he didn't have any personal animosity against the students at the football game, but said that it is "not racist to point out that we should be favoring Texans over foreigners" and that his fellow Republicans are afraid of being called racist.

The divide emerging among Texas Republicans over the social media post — and Democrats' eagerness to capitalize on it — show just how precarious the party finds its position this cycle. Texas Republicans were already worrying about losing support from Hispanic and other minority voters amid a tough economic environment and President Donald Trump's unpopular immigration agenda. They need to hold onto or improve the incremental gains they made over previous cycles with voters of color in a fast-changing state where non-Hispanic white people now only make up 37% of the population. The stakes are high this cycle: Most polls show Paxton slightly trailing in a Senate race that could determine control of the upper chamber; Abbott appears to be in the toughest of his four election fights; and the state is home to several key House races.

"I don't think [French's post] independently and universally sours voter sentiment. But it contributes to GOP declining numbers with Hispanic voters particularly in the South Texas congressional races which we hope to win," said Alfredo Rodriguez, a Dallas-based Republican strategist, who called on French to "stop the petty political theatrics."

The blast radius of French's posts was wide enough to garner carefully worded responses from the top of the ticket. Abbott said in a Sunday statement that French's post "is not my message," before noting unity "doesn't mean that Texas cannot also lead in having the toughest immigration laws of any state in America and freezing H1B visas at our universities."

Two of the students in the photo told the Dallas Morning News that they're U.S. citizens. Most UT students are Texans — state law requires that 90% of each freshman class come from in-state — and there is no evidence that the students in the photo French posted are foreigners.

Some Republicans weren't thrilled about Abbott's response.

"This had nothing to do with illegal immigrants," said Anang Mittal, an Indian American national GOP strategist, of Abbott's comments. "These were students at a college game. They're not H-1B. If they're students, they're on a student visa. … It's pretty damn disgusting of Greg Abbott to say, 'I condemn racism, but also, like, we're keeping all the Indians out.' That's essentially what that tweet read to me."Democrat James Talarico called Paxton out on social media, asking if he would follow Cornyn's lead in denouncing French's post. The GOP nominee replied that he condemns "racism in all its forms" — and then claimed Talarico had a "history of dividing Texans by race."

Spokespeople for Paxton and Abbott did not respond to requests for comment.

Other Republicans were less willing to fully denounce French's comments.

"I don't really know the guy. I heard he said some not so pleasant things," said Rep. Troy Nehls (R-Texas), who said he hadn't seen the posts — but launched into a criticism of immigration nonetheless. "I am concerned about the number of people living in this country, and we don't even know who they really are," he said. "Shut the border down for 10 years, and then let's try to figure out who we got in this country because we don't even know."

Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.), who campaigned with Talarico in Houston on Sunday, said French's posts came up in conversations with every Asian American voter he met.

"Everyone was talking about it," Kim said. "Every single Asian American that I was with yesterday raised this with me. They were saying this is an example of, 'Not only are they not courting us or engaging with us, but they're actively demonizing us, actively being xenophobic and racist towards us.' We need leaders that stand up against this."

The political damage could also extend — potentially for years — to Texas' small but growing Indian American population, the demographic group French appeared to target in his posts. Both Dallas and Houston have significant Indian American populations. In 2019, an event at a Houston stadium headlined by Trump and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi drew over 50,000 attendees.

French's comments could alienate those same voters, said Brendan Steinhauser, a Republican consultant in Austin.

"He just irritated a bunch of people, many of whom could be supporters and could be Republicans," said Steinhauser, a University of Texas graduate. "I'd be willing to bet a lot of those kids that he was posting a photo of are probably, you know, their parents might be Republicans, or they might be Republicans, or conservatives, or independent-leaning conservatives."

If French is elected, he would sit on a commission that regulates Texas' powerful oil, gas and mining industries — which has little to do with immigration or social issues. But French, a longtime provocateur in Texas political circles, has a history of incendiary statements. Just last year, Republicans were calling on French to resign as chair of the Tarrant County Republican Party after he published an online poll asking whether Muslims or Jews were "the bigger threat to America." He deleted the post and said he regretted it, adding "antisemitism has no place in the Republican Party." This spring, he unseated a well-financed Republican incumbent for Texas Railroad Commission.

French isn't the only politician in Texas who has made singling out Muslims part of his political brand. Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick has made "preventing Shariah law in Texas" one of his legislative priorities. Patrick didn't respond to a request for comment. Abbott, Paxton and Cornyn have all called for investigations and other government action to stop development of a commercial and residential development being built by the East Plano Islamic Center, a mosque outside Dallas. And just last month, Abbott threatened to withhold funding from Dallas Fort Worth International Airport to block plans for ritual washing facilities for Muslim travelers in the airport's terminals. There's little difference between French's attacks and the other politicians' actions, said Yasir Qadhi, an Islamic scholar at the Islamic center."It is the same mindset," he said in an interview. "What we're witnessing is really an unprecedented and increasingly brazen form of racism. It's unfiltered, it's unapologetic, it's even stripped of even the pretense of political correctness. You know, this is a type of racism we've never seen in our lifetimes."

When French unleashed a string of inflammatory social media posts in 2025, several GOP officeholders — including Patrick, the lieutenant governor — called on him to resign as county GOP chair. But Republicans now refuse to tell French to drop out now "because that might mean that there would be a Democrat elected statewide," said Glen Whitley, a Republican former Tarrant County judge. "That's the bottom line."

"That's part of my frustration with the Republican Party altogether: They talk about being Christian, but they get up every morning to talk about who they hate," said Whitley, who still identifies as Republican but endorsed Talarico for Senate.

Joey Fox contributed to this report.

title: McDermott wants to commit to England for 2030 World Cup
description: Brian McDermott says he wants to stay on as England's head coach for the 2030 Rugby League World Cup.
fullText:
Brian McDermott says he wants to stay on as England's head coach for the 2030 Rugby League World Cup.

The former Leeds Rhinos head coach, 56, was appointed on a short-term agreement in April to guide England through this autumn's World Cup, which is taking place in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

McDermott said when he started in the job that he would be interested in staying on beyond the tournament.

And although he has made clear that he wants to focus on the immediate task of seeking success this October and November, he does want to commit to his country for the long term if all goes well.

He said: "Well, we've had a very informal discussion about what that might look like and then that's all it is. And it's been a really short conversation.

"Clearly, I'd like to do the job for longer. I'd like to get another crack at the World Cup in four years' time.

"You know, if you're going to do this properly, give me four years' preparation, where we're building it up year by year and getting players connected to a programme which has got a start, a middle and the end."

McDermott, currently working as an assistant coach at NRL club Gold Coast Titans, has taken the England role on a part-time basis, in contrast to his full-time predecessor Shaun Wane.

He has confirmed Wigan great Sean O'Loughlin and St Helens legend Paul Wellens as assistant coaches for the World Cup.

And he believes England are well set for it, but having had only a limited time to prepare - with no matches before their World Cup opener against Tonga in Perth on 17 October - he would like a chance to have a full build-up to a major tournament.

He said: "This has been a crazy, crazy period over the last few months to try and coordinate all this. And I think we're in good shape, by the way.

"But yeah, I've made it no secret. I'd like a crack at the next World Cup and a four-year build-up to that.

"We haven't gone too deep into those discussions. And when you mention it, you think, no, let's not talk about that. I've got to get my mind on this here. So it has been mentioned, but I'm not chasing that just yet."

New England boss McDermott offers route back for Connor

Rhinos dominate 2026 Super League Dream Team

McDermott said when he took the job that he intended to stick with George Williams as captain.

The Warrington half-back, who will leave Super League for NRL club Dolphins after the World Cup, returned to action in August after four months out with a neck injury.

Having got to know Williams during that time, McDermott is happy to have him leading the team.

"He's been great to speak to," McDermott said. "I didn't really know George at all.

"It's been really enjoyable to get to know him. He's keen as anything.

"And while he was injured, you could just tell he came back from injury early, but you could tell if there's anybody who's going to come back from it early, it would be him.

"And I'm really pleased to see the form that he's in now.

"His leadership's been really good. When we've had the groups meetings, I saw the way he would speak on there and just have a bit of maturity.

title: Wales lose injured Powell for entire WXV campaign

fullText:
Wales have been dealt another injury blow before their WXV Global Series campaign with Harlequins' Kayleigh Powell ruled out of the entire tournament.

The 27-year-old sevens Olympian was a standout player at full-back during the Six Nations and impressed at fly-half when Wales ended their nine match losing streak against the Barbarians in June.

But she will sit out Wales' Tests against South Africa, USA and Japan after suffering a hamstring injury in training.

Powell wrote on her social media that she was "absolutely gutted" to be missing the campaign, but has "every faith that this team will do great things."

Head coach Sean Lynn is already without Premiership Women's Rugby (PRW) title-winning prop Donna Rose, while backs Carys Cox and Nel Metcalfe have only just returned to training.

Lleucu George could slot back in at 10, while scrum-half Keira Bevan provides Lynn another option having trained there during pre-season.

title: US acknowledges for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space
description: The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.  Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told the Air and Space Cyber Conference in Maryland on Monday that the U.S. ha...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States has confirmed for the first time that it has deployed weapons in space.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told the Air and Space Cyber Conference in Maryland on Monday that the U.S. has fielded "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action."

Meink did not detail what the weapons were or how they work. In 2024 the U.S. said Russia was developing a new anti-satellite weapon that could be launched from space. At the time the White House said the danger wasn't imminent.

But reports of the anti-satellite weapon reflected longstanding worries about space threats from Russia and China, given that much U.S. infrastructure is dependent on satellite communications.

In his remarks, Meink also said the Air Force was adding more autonomous systems to its capabilities and predicted the service would look "radically different" by 2032. For example, he foresaw one-way attack drones replacing artillery as the "primary killer."

"We are increasing readiness against existing threats," he said.

Trump created the Space Force in 2019.

title: The 'Brampton bagsman' taking Championship by storm
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the scintillating form of Southampton's 'Brampton bagsman' Cyle Larin.
fullText:
Not many forwards in world football have had a better start to their season than Southampton's Cyle Larin.

The Canada striker is the leading goalscorer in the Championship and has netted more than anyone in Europe's top five leagues.

He may have played more games than the stars from the Premier League and La Liga, but his seven goals in seven league matches have caught the eye.

His average of 73 minutes per goal is better than the 75 Kylian Mbappe is averaging for Real Madrid and Erling Haaland's 90 minutes per strike in the Premier League for Manchester City.

Larin's exploits have even led Saints head coach Tonda Eckert to label him "the best striker in the league" - lofty praise in a division that also boasts Jarrod Bowen, Raul Jimenez, Mohamed Toure and the emerging Will Lankshear.

But it is not just favouritism from his manager - neutral plaudits, including August's Championship Player of the Month award, are also landing at his feet.

The 'Brampton bagsman' - a nickname coined from his Ontario hometown - has helped propel Eckert's team from bottom of the table on minus four points to inside the top eight with 10.

Saints would be second, behind West Ham on goal difference, if not for the points deduction that came as punishment for the Spygate scandal.

But after a nomadic career that has taken in spells in the United States, Turkey, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands, why has Larin been so effective for the south coast side?

Since signing for Southampton on an initial loan from Mallorca in early 2026, Larin's first venture into English football has been an impactful one.

The 31-year-old netted three minutes into his Saints debut last season, going on to finish with eight Championship goals in 16 games during the second half of the campaign.

Following the fall-out from Spygate, he did not get the chance to help Southampton reach the Premier League but had to quickly turn his attention to the World Cup and representing his country as one of the host nations.

He shone for Canada on the biggest of stages, scoring two goals - one a crucial late equaliser against Bosnia-Herzegovina - as Jesse Marsch's side reached the last 16 before losing to Morocco.

Larin's contribution for Canada as their second all-time leading goalscorer has even earned him a key to his home city of Brampton,, external something he will collect during the upcoming international break.

Back on English soil, Larin has been even more prolific for Saints than he was last term, scoring eight times in nine appearances across all competitions.

However, the forward has been quick to point out it has been far from a solo effort.

"It feels good but I don't think I can do this without my team-mates," he told BBC Radio Solent after scoring twice in the 4-1 win over Bristol City on Saturday.

"They play such a big role in me being able to score and I have to give credit to the coach too, he's given me the role to play free up there and that's what I'm doing.

"It's the beginning of the season and we have to keep working hard as we have a long way to go. You can't get too high after these games, you have to be level-headed."

Larin has a point - in Finn Azaz and Leo Scienza, who boast five goals and six assists between them already this term, he has two of the division's best creators a striker could wish for.

Eckert hails 'best in the league' Larin

Does Larin need more help up top?

Last season, he shared the minutes up front with Ross Stewart but with the Scot now at Swansea and Larin clearly the first choice at St Mary's, he has been taking advantage of more minutes on the pitch.

Larin rarely completes 90 minutes with Eckert tending to prefer to withdraw him during the second half - and that makes his statistics even more impressive.

He is averaging 1.23 goals per 90 minutes, scoring every 73 minutes with a goal conversion rate of 25% - seven goals from 28 shots.

Only one other striker - Norwich's Mathias Kvistgaarden (1.27) - has a better goal per 90 minutes rate and only Bowen (29) has attempted more shots.

"When you have quality footballers like Larin then you get goals," former Saints midfielder Jo Tessem said on the latest episode of BBC Radio Solent's Goin' Home.

"Quality players like him step up when you need them and so far this season he's done that.

"Eckert has said that Larin has been a lot fitter right now than when he arrived in January and that has made a difference so far."

There's a simplicity to Cyle Larin's game - and understanding that has underpinned Southampton's strong start to the campaign.

Rarely tasked with dropping into the build-up, he hangs on the opposition's last line, ready to make powerful runs into the channels.

Tonda Eckert has asked fans to trust Saints when they build from the back, with Larin's movement a significant reason why.

If his team-mates play through the press, he has the space to stretch defences and finish off swift counter attacks.

Larin has stressed the help of his team-mates too.

The immediacy of his runs creates the room for Azaz between the lines and for the combinations between the pair that preceded Larin's opening goal against Bristol City, for example.

Finding space in crowded situations, though - especially for a side who want to dominate possession - is equally crucial for a centre-forward.

Larin's instinctive movement and clever body usage offer a potent mix of snappy shots off either foot, aerial threat and those tricks of the trade the 31-year-old has picked up over the years.

A Larin trademark is drifting to the back post, a magnet for the crossing quality of right-back James Bree.

He is low touch, high impact - but that's just the system Eckert wants around his main man.

title: A team in form - how Farke has turned Leeds around
description: With Leeds United third in the Premier League, BBC Sport assesses their improvement under Daniel Farke.
fullText:
As the nascent Premier League table takes shape, the sight of Leeds United in third place feels like a throwback to the turn of the century, when they secured five top-five finishes on the bounce.

Monday's 4-1 home win over Newcastle United means Daniel Farke's unbeaten side have made their best start to a top-flight season since 2001-02 under David O'Leary.

In truth, Leeds, with eight points from four games, have been playing well for some time, and it can all be traced back to a bold change of formation by Farke almost nine months ago.

The German switched from a back four to a back three at half-time against Manchester City on 29 November, a game in which his team battled back from 2-0 down at the break to level things at 2-2 before conceding in stoppage time at Etihad Stadium.

Starting with the subsequent home win over Chelsea on 3 December, Leeds have lost only five of their past 29 league games, results which would place them fifth in the hypothetical league table for that timeframe.

So how have they done it? And can they push for European football for the first time in 24 years?

In the 2025 summer transfer window Farke and the club's new sporting director Adam Underwood made a point of signing tall players who could "add a special physicality" to the squad they were building for the robust demands of the English top flight.

Of the 10 permanent arrivals, eight – Jaka Bijol, Sebastiaan Bornauw, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, James Justin, Lukas Nmecha, Noah Okafor, Lucas Perri and Anton Stach – stand more than 6ft tall.

Speaking in July 2025, Farke said: "I wouldn't say it's coincidence that they are all tall players but, of course, if you join the Premier League and you have one of the smallest groups, you expect that probably there is more pressure on you than there was in the Championship. You have to make sure that you're also good in defending crosses."

This summer, after losing centre-back Pascal Struijk to Brighton, Farke moved for two World Cup players - Bosnia-Herzegovina's Tarik Muharemovic and Switzerland's Nico Elvedi - to bolster his defence.

Despite an error leading to Bazoumana Toure's late consolation goal for Newcastle, Muharemovic has looked particularly impressive, playing every league minute in front of 6ft 5in England international James Trafford, who became the most expensive British goalkeeper in history for the second time when he joined for an initial £40m from City.

Throw in Harry Wilson, one of the league's standout players last season, who joined on a free transfer from Fulham, and Leeds' latest signings look to be particularly shrewd.

Leeds lost eight of their first 13 league games in 2025-26, leaving them in 18th position and facing the very real prospect of relegation.

Reports at the time suggested Farke, whose side had pipped Burnley to the Championship title the previous season, was in real danger of losing his job.

While the rejig clearly had its intended effect on the Leeds defence – among the ever-present clubs in the division, only champions Arsenal, City and Nottingham Forest have conceded fewer goals since the switch – it has helped in other areas too.

The most notable beneficiary has been Dominic Calvert-Lewin. Since last December only Erling Haaland, Ollie Watkins and Joao Pedro have scored more top-flight goals than Calvert-Lewin's 14.

Having toiled as the lone centre-forward in a 4-3-3 formation, relying on infrequent support from out wide, Calvert-Lewin has thrived with a proper strike partner, often in the form of Nmecha or Okafor, who boasts seven goals and an assist in his past 11 league appearances.

Although Farke still finds himself alternating between 3-4-3 and 3-5-2, Calvert-Lewin himself has said: "I enjoy having bodies around me."

With Crystal Palace the visitors to Elland Road on Saturday, Calvert-Lewin is aiming to become the first Leeds player to score in six consecutive league home games since Arthur Hydes in 1932.

The former Everton forward missed out on a place in England's World Cup squad but, with three goals in all competitions this season, he is surely in with a chance of an international recall on Friday as Thomas Tuchel prepares for the Nations League quadruple-header.

Elland Road was bouncing on Monday night as the vast majority of the 36,693 fans savoured Leeds' stunning performance.

The famous old ground has been something of a fortress under the lights in recent seasons. Before consecutive losses to City and Sunderland in February, Leeds had gone 25 evening kick-offs in league and play-off games without a home defeat, winning 20 and drawing five.

The thumping win over Newcastle meant their new manager, Matthias Jaissle, became the latest coach to be welcomed to what Leeds fans call 'Daniel Farke Penitentiary'.

The online meme – in which managers defeated by Farke are 'sentenced' to time in his fictional prison – flooded social media again after the game.

Farke enjoyed the adulation of the supporters at full-time and, while he has quite rightly played down early talk of European qualification, a continuation of this form will have the Elland Road faithful dreaming of a return to those famous Champions League nights of a quarter of a century ago.

title: Eligibility rules 'not particularly fair' - O'Neill
description: Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill says what upsets him the most regarding rules over international eligibility is the pressure put on young players to make an irreversible choice.
fullText:
Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill said what upsets him the most regarding rules over international eligibility is the pressure put on young players to make an irreversible choice.

Any player born in Northern Ireland is also eligible to play for the Republic of Ireland, but Fifa rules state that an application to transfer international allegiance can only be made once.

The situation has again been in the spotlight with regards to Arsenal teenager Ceadach O'Neill who has won two senior caps for Northern Ireland and on Tuesday was included in the squad for a Nations League quadruple-header, but has also been subject to an approach from the Republic of Ireland.

At present, the player would be required to undertake a Fifa transfer of international allegiance should he wish to play for the Republic of Ireland at any level, but if he makes an appearance in the upcoming Nations League quadruple header, would have to wait until he is 21 to do so. Should he reach four caps, he would be unable to transfer at any stage.

"My focus is on the player, and I have a duty of care to the player as his international manager, as we have as an association as well," said Michael O'Neill.

"He's been in our pathway since he's been a young boy. He's been part of our academy. He's obviously had an approach from another association, which happens.

"The thing that upsets me the most in this is that putting a young player in a position to make an international transfer before he's been a professional for even two years is, I think, not the right thing. It's not something that any association should be doing."

O'Neill and Graham retain places in NI squad

Arsenal have 'big hopes' for O'Neill - Arteta

Under the Good Friday Agreement - the 1998 peace accord that followed the conflict colloquially known as The Troubles - those born in Northern Ireland can hold both British and Irish passports.

A Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling in 2010 means players born anywhere on the island of Ireland are able to represent the Republic of Ireland regardless of whether they fulfil any other measure of eligibility, namely being born in the territory, having a biological mother, father, grandmother or grandfather born in the territory, or having lived there for an uninterrupted period of five years.

Players born in the Republic of Ireland, however, cannot represent Northern Ireland unless they are otherwise eligible.

"We exploit eligibility, the same as every other country does, down to the grandparent rule, but this is a rule which is obviously unique between ourselves and the FAI [Football Association of Ireland]," said O'Neill.

"I think everyone recognises it's not particularly fair, but as I say, our focus is to make sure our pathway for our young players is as good as possible and that's a pathway for boys from any part of the community."

In May, FAI director of football John Martin said the organisation should at "the bare minimum" be sounding out eligible players.

"We know there are kids out there who want to play for Ireland who haven't been approached in the past," said Martin.

"That's not right. It's making sure we have a presence and we understand all the players available to us, and that they are being monitored and tracked."

When asked whether the narrative around young players in or around his squad is tiresome to him, O'Neill said: "It would have been in the past, it's not tiresome now.

"We have people who comment on this and talk about nationality and talk about identity and talk about all these different things, which are part of being born in Northern Ireland and growing up in Northern Ireland.

"But I think what we're missing now is that we're putting young players in a situation where they have to make a decision which is irreversible."

During O'Neill's time as manager, Tottenham Hotspur's Jamie Donley and Gillingham's Ronan Hale have made international transfers to Northern Ireland from England and the Republic of Ireland respectively.

"We've done two international transfers in my time. Jamie Donley, who is now a senior international, and Ronan Hale, who was 25 at the time when we asked him to make that decision," added O'Neill.

"I think there's a point in a player's career where you've just got to let him play and develop, enjoy his football without creating a situation like this.

"We haven't created this situation. Ceadach's been in our system all along and he's in our squad now."

While James McClean and Shane Duffy are the two most prominent examples of players who made the switch from Northern Ireland at underage level and went on to have long international careers for the Republic of Ireland, O'Neill believes others would have won considerably more caps for his side.

"I think if you look at it from our point of view, there's not many players that have been a success who have gone from Northern Ireland," he said.

"I can think of two, James McClean and Shane Duffy, who had international careers where they got over 50 caps. Otherwise, most of the other players who have gone that route have not played consistently or not had, I think, possibly the international career they could have had if they stayed here.

"It is a decision for the player to make, ultimately, and we have to respect that, but as I've said all along, I think there's two sides to this. There is obviously who you feel you should play for, but there's also the situation around a football decision where you can have longevity in your international career."

title: Celtic & Scotland legend McGrain diagnosed with Alzheimer's
description: Danny McGrain, described by Celtic as "Scotland's greatest-ever full-back", has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, his family confirms.
fullText:
Danny McGrain, described by Celtic as "Scotland's greatest-ever full-back", has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, his family has confirmed.

Speaking to the club's website, wife Laraine McGrain said she wanted to explain why the 76-year-old had become less involved with the Scottish champions and their fans.

"Danny received this diagnosis some time ago and, as time has moved on, we felt it was right to be open and clear," she said.

"Danny has always loved helping supporters - whether through hospital visits, assisting fans with charity events, or sending messages of support.

"As time has gone on, that has become more difficult for Danny, so we wanted to explain his situation with honesty and with the care and respect the Celtic family has always shown us."

Why does Sutton have 'great concerns' about Celtic?

McGregor laments Celtic's 'team of individuals'

McGrain, who played 62 times for Scotland, came through Celtic's youth ranks and spent 17 years with the Glasgow club.

He had one season with Hamilton Academical before ending his distinguished career in 1988 and going on to manage Arbroath for two seasons.

Celtic point out that he "remained a constant presence at Celtic over the years through a range of coaching roles, supporting our youth development programme via Celtic Pools and hosting hospitality at Celtic Park".

"In recent weeks, Laraine and their daughters, Vicki, Dawn and Carly, decided they wanted to be open with supporters so that Danny can continue to receive the love and support of the Celtic family, just as he has given so freely and humbly to others throughout his life," the club state.

"Despite the changes this diagnosis has brought, Danny remains in good spirits, enjoying time with his loved ones, following the game and staying close to the club he holds so dear."

As a player, McGrain became a Celtic legend, with the club pointing out that "he was widely considered by football experts, journalists, and peers to be the finest right-back in world football during the 1970s".

Overall, he played 663 games for Celtic between 1970 and 1987, winning seven League Championships, five Scottish Cups and two Scottish League Cups before helping Accies win promotion to the top flight in his final season.
